entries.title: As freed ComEd defendants face new trial, jurors say they already considered ‘every aspect’ of the case
entries.summary: <p>Before they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2026/04/14/madigan-bribery-comed-conspiracy-bribery-chicago-crime-pramaggiore-mcclain" target="_blank" >freed two former ComEd officials</a> who went to prison over an alleged corruption scheme<b> </b>involving Illinois’ most powerful politician, federal appeals court judges asked a lot of questions about the case — but mostly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/11/3/23919713/corruption-jurors-ed-burke-trial" target="_blank" >about the jury</a> that found the pair guilty.</p><p>For example, how could the judges be sure the jury didn’t focus solely on bribery claims that have since been undermined by the U.S. Supreme Court?</p><p>The Chicago Sun-Times asked three of the 12 jurors Wednesday. They said they carefully considered every claim leveled against former ComEd CEO Anne<b> </b>Pramaggiore and longtime ComEd lobbyist Michael McClain — including those that survived a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2024/06/26/supreme-court-snyder-ruling-madigan-corruption" target="_blank" >2024 Supreme Court ruling</a>.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2026/04/14/madigan-bribery-comed-conspiracy-bribery-chicago-crime-pramaggiore-mcclain" >Ex-ComEd CEO, Madigan ally to be freed from prison as appeals court calls for new trial in conspiracy case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“We concluded they all intertwined and related to each other,” Robert<b> </b>Garnes, one of the jurors in the 2023 ComEd conspiracy trial, told the Sun-Times.</p><p>The ComEd trial <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/5/2/23697452/jurors-reach-verdict-in-comed-bribery-trial" target="_blank" >ended with the convictions</a> of McClain, Pramaggiore<b> </b>and two others of a plot to bribe<b> </b>ex-Illinois House Speaker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news" target="_blank" >Michael J. Madigan</a>. The high court’s later decision to limit a key bribery law undermined the verdict and led to the dismissal of the bribery counts in 2025. But convictions for conspiracy and falsifying books and records remained.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Then the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals took things further Tuesday. It promised to order a new trial and told the feds to release Pramaggiore and McClain from their two-year prison sentences “forthwith.”<b> </b>The news came four hours after a three-judge panel heard arguments in the case.</p><p>The Federal Bureau of Prisons confirmed the release of McClain and Pramaggiore late Wednesday afternoon.</p><p>The appeals court’s order had no direct impact on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news/mike-madigan-guilty-verdict" target="_blank" >Madigan’s separate conviction</a>, which came in February 2025. The 2023 trial of McClain and Pramaggiore also ended with the convictions of longtime ComEd lobbyist John Hooker and former City Club President Jay Doherty, but they did not appeal and have served their sentences.</p><p>During Tuesday’s arguments in the ComEd case, Judges<b> </b>Thomas<b> </b>Kirsch<b> </b>and<b> </b>Joshua<b> </b>Kolar<b> </b>seemed particularly concerned with the remaining conspiracy conviction against McClain and Pramaggiore.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/11/3/23919713/corruption-jurors-ed-burke-trial" >‘Facts and common sense’: Chicago’s corruption jurors reflect on past trials as Ed Burke’s case nears</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>It featured multiple “objects”<b> </b>for the jury to consider, including bribery and falsifying records.</p><p>Given the feds’ emphasis on bribery during the trial, as well as the Supreme Court’s ruling, the judges wanted assurance that jurors reached a verdict that included false records as an object of the conspiracy, rather than an invalid bribery theory.</p><p>“Here’s the problem,” Kirsch told a prosecutor. “When you charge the case and try the case as a bribery case, what’s to say the jury just didn’t consider the illegal bribery object in the conspiracy and stop right there?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatLeft> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure “was actually one of the last ones we looked at,” even though it appeared as Count One<b> </b>in the indictment.</p><p>“That was the big behemoth of it all,” Goldenberg said. “We actually did really parse it out and look at each individual charge and looked at each object of it.”</p><p>Another juror, Amanda<b> </b>Schnitker Sayers, agreed with Goldenberg’s recollection. She said, “we almost worked it backwards” during the 27-hour deliberations.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2026/04/14/madigan-bribery-comed-conspiracy-bribery-chicago-crime-pramaggiore-mcclain" >Ex-ComEd CEO, Madigan ally to be freed from prison as appeals court calls for new trial in conspiracy case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“For each individual count we took them all separate and we went through and we found the evidence for each one,” Schnitker Sayers said.</p><p>Garnes said it all “went hand in hand.”</p><p>“We took in every aspect of the trial that was presented before us,” he said.</p><p>The jurors’ comments are unlikely to influence what happens next in the case. entries.title: Sky's Skylar Diggins wanted to be closer to home, but she’s not just coasting into retirement
entries.summary: <p>To be a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> fan right now is to be bursting with questions. Ones like: What is Skylar Diggins doing in Chicago?</p><p>It surprised many to see the seven-time All-Star choose a team that has won less than 30% of its games over the last two seasons, and an organization not exactly known for flawless execution since its 2021 championship.</p><p>So how did she end up here?</p><p>As the new collective-bargaining agreement reshaped the league this offseason, Diggins took a moment to reflect.</p><p>She thought about where she was in her career — 35 years old, two kids, entering her 12th season — and decided she wanted a change. She's played on the West Coast her whole career, but she grew up in South Bend, 90 miles outside of Chicago.</p><p>She wanted to be closer to home.</p><p>And Chicago successfully sold her on its vision: a win-now roster that was tougher, more athletic, more competitive than last year.</p><p>For head coach Tyler Marsh, Diggins' arrival is proof the organization is moving in the right direction.</p><p>"Skylar has been around this league a long time to know the fake from the real," Marsh said. "And there's a reason she wanted to be here. Being close to home helps, but you also gotta be able to trust the people you're going to compete with. There's some discernment there that she's able to recognize."</p><p>The Sky did execute well in free agency, landing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/04/14/azura-stevens-returns-to-chicago-where-the-fit-and-the-money-made-sense" >stretch big Azurá Stevens</a> and two-way wing DiJonai Carrington, and adding young talent in Rickea Jackson and Jacy Sheldon.</p><p>But executing the "win-now" part won't be easy. Most of the league's top teams retained their cores. And even with all the added talent, Diggins is still the Sky's only All-Star.</p><p>Which means the Sky better hope she didn't come back to the Midwest just to decompress before retiring.</p><p>Lucky for them, she shot down the idea before anyone thought to raise it.</p><p>"I'm not just coming here saying this is the end or whatever for me," she said at her introductory news conference. "I don't think it'll be a diminishing return. I'm committed to the work. … I want to get better. That's been my mantra since I was a kid — 'get better.' That's the mindset I have here for this organization, for myself, and that's the standard I hold myself to."</p><p>Even for players with the highest standards, some decline in their game is inevitable. Over the last two years, Diggins' scoring average has settled around 15, down from the 17-20 range of her prime. But pair that with six assists and you're still looking at one of the best point guards in the league.</p><p>So, Sky fans: is this great-player-comes-home-at-the-tail-end-of-her-career storyline giving anyone a Candace Parker flashback? Will this homecoming end in a championship, too?</p><p>One can hope. But there are a few big differences between then and now. As good as Diggins is, she's not quite Parker. And Parker came home to a roster that had been together for years. Diggins is walking into a complete overhaul.</p><p>She'll need a little magic to bring them together ahead of schedule.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module entries.title: After quick struggles for Shane Smith, White Sox aim to 'slow down his world' at Triple-A
entries.summary: <p>After an awful opening week, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a>’ starting rotation has been a bright spot with an MLB-best 1.73 ERA in 11 games from April 3-14.</p><p>If you were told in spring training that Sox starters would go on a heater like that, you probably would’ve expected Opening Day hurler <b>Shane Smith </b>to be on top of his game — not down on the farm trying to rediscover his All-Star form from last season.</p><p>For Smith to run it back to the big leagues, he’s got to stop running away from the pitch that made him a Rule 5 success story, general manager <b>Chris Getz</b> said a week after the surprising demotion.</p><p>“He was running away from using his four-seam fastball. Just the overall quality of that pitch, along with his curveball, just wasn't up to his standard,” Getz said of the righty, who covered only 8⅓ innings in his three Sox starts, surrendering 12 runs before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports/2026/04/08/white-sox-option-opening-day-starter-shane-smith-to-triple-a-charlotte" target="_blank" ><u>getting shipped to Triple-A Charlotte</u></a>. “We felt like it was best to kind of slow down his world a little bit, get him in an environment that is not so focused on getting so deep into games, or even win the ballgame."</p><p>Smith looked a little better in his last big-league game, but had another uneven outing in his first go with the Knights over the weekend, giving up three runs on four hits with a walk and five strikeouts in four innings.</p><p>“There’s always a cascade effect when you have starters not going deep into games. It starts affecting bullpens,” Getz said. “He definitely made progress in the most recent outing up here at the major league level, but we know that he can be so much better, and he acknowledges that as well.”</p><h3><b>Pre-game scare</b></h3><p>Attendees at Rate Field were left in a stunned silence before Wednesday’s game when <b>Gerald Chaney</b> collapsed while singing "Lift Every Voice and Sing” on Jackie Robinson Day.</p><p>Chaney, a longtime national anthem performer and beloved ballpark presence, was alert as paramedics treated him on the field. He was taken to a hospital for further evaluation and treatment, according to the Sox.</p><h3><b>Schultz in the rotation</b></h3><p>Manager <b>Will Venable</b> confirmed that rookie lefty <b>Noah Schultz</b> has a regular spot in the Sox’ starting rotation after his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/14/noah-schultz-white-sox-mlb-debut" target="_blank" ><u>shaky MLB debut</u></a> Tuesday night — no surprise, but an assertion that Getz stopped short of making a day earlier.</p><p>Schultz consistently flashed 98 on the radar gun and struck out four while laboring through 4⅓ innings, giving up four runs but rebounding from some first-inning jitters.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure in the big leagues."</p><p>Soft-spoken in the clubhouse but intense on the mound, the 6-10 Schultz credited big sisters <b>Emily Schultz</b> and <b>Ashley Schultz</b> with sharpening his on-field edge in their childhood Wiffle ball games in the backyard while <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/13/noah-schultz-white-sox-debut-aurora-oswego-east" target="_blank" ><u>growing up in Aurora</u></a>.</p><p>“They helped get that competitive spirit in me. It started at a young age,” Schultz said. “I can’t thank them enough. They have been with me through it all. It’s so awesome to have their support and have them in the stands.”</p><h3><b>Coming and going</b></h3><p>As part of the Sox’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/15/sam-antonacci-called-up-white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>latest roster shuffle</u></a> bringing up prospect <b>Sam Antonacci</b>, they also recalled veteran lefty reliever <b>Tyler Gilbert</b>, optioned <b>Brandon Eisert</b> to Charlotte and designated outfielder <b>Dustin Harris</b> for assignment.</p><p>Harris was a hero of Sunday’s win at Kansas City, robbing a potential home run in right field. He went 3-for-12 with a double, four walks and a pair of stolen bases in six games with the Sox.</p><p>Venable said they’ll send him to Charlotte if he clears waivers.</p><p>“It was a really tough decision. … He was really just kind of the odd guy out, really not because of anything he did,” Venable said.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: White Sox national anthem performer Gerald Chaney back to singing after pre-game collapse
entries.summary: <p>Attendees at Rate Field were left in a stunned silence before Wednesday’s White Sox game when Gerald Chaney collapsed while singing “Lift Every Voice and Sing” on Jackie Robinson Day.</p><p>Chaney, a longtime national anthem performer and beloved ballpark presence, was alert as paramedics treated him on the field. He was taken to a hospital for evaluation and doing well by the end of the game — “even singing,” according to the Sox.</p><p>“The entire White Sox family is sending love to Gerald and his family for a full and speedy recovery,” the team said in a statement.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-600000" name="image-600000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e88797b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F10%2Fa7%2F3c33490947b3a7b987657b17d485%2Fsox-cst-062412-4.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/51cfee9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F10%2Fa7%2F3c33490947b3a7b987657b17d485%2Fsox-cst-062412-4.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fc0eb07/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F10%2Fa7%2F3c33490947b3a7b987657b17d485%2Fsox-cst-062412-4.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Gerald Chaney, pictured singing the national anthem before a Sox game on June 22, 2012. I think everyone did a great job in responding and did the best to make sure he was alright. So, really good news to hear that he is alright.”</p><p>Sox starter Sean Burke was warming up when the medical emergency unfolded.</p><p>“They said he's doing well at the hospital now, so hopefully he's going to make a full recovery from that,” Burke said. "I was just trying to make sure he was all good, first and foremost.”</p>

entries.title: White Sox call up Sam Antonacci looking for jolt to stagnant offense
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> prospect Sam Antonacci got news of his promotion from Triple-A Charlotte about 20 hours before he took the field for his debut at Rate Field on Wednesday. </p><p>“Tired, but adrenaline high,” the Springfield native said inside his first big-league clubhouse after a whirlwind travel day. “Get a cup of coffee in you and you’re good to go.”</p><p>It worked for him while playing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/19/sam-antonacci-returns-to-spring-training-says-wbc-experience-was-definitely-worth-it" >for Team Italy</a>, whose run to the World Baseball Classic semifinal was famously fueled by a dugout espresso machine also enjoyed by another caffeine-cranked Sox player, Kyle Teel.</p><p>Now the Sox are looking for a shot in the arm offensively from Antonacci, a utility player whose hot bat to start the year made him the club’s second key prospect call-up in as many days, following the debut of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/14/noah-schultz-white-sox-mlb-debut" target="_blank" ><u>prized left-hander Noah Schultz</u></a>.</p><p>“Excited to add his energy and his skillset to the group,” manager Will Venable said. “He's gonna play extremely hard, control the zone, play solid defense and run the bases extremely well.”</p><p>The Sox’ No. 9-rated prospect wasted little time checking some of those boxes with his parents, sister and 10,192 of his newest fans in attendance. Antonacci vacuumed up a grounder to second base for his first big-league defensive assist to close the first inning, and then dropped a single into right field in his first career at-bat to open the Sox’ half of the second on Wednesday against the Rays. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">First big league hit for Sam Antonacci! <a href="https://t.co/p2h7zrD4DF">pic.twitter.com/p2h7zrD4DF</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://twitter.com/whitesox/status/2044572659208400997?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 16, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Later in his 1-for-3 night, he made a diving stop on a hot grounder up the middle, and drew a ninth-inning walk that started the Sox' only offensive onslaught during an otherwise lifeless 8-3 loss that saw catcher Reese McGuire pitching in garbage time.</p><p>"It was a dream come true, to be honest. Obviously not the end result," Antonacci said. "As much as I like to be even-keeled and keep my head on straight with the job at task, I needed to take a step back and really take it all in, because I’m living out a dream I had when I was a little kid."</p><p>Though the 2024 fifth-round draft pick debuted at second, he got to the Sox three weeks into the season because he was learning left field on the job at Charlotte, fast-tracking his path in an organization lacking outfield depth. Antonacci mostly played second last year across three levels of the farm system. </p><p>Venable said he had him batting fifth and playing second in his debut only because it coincided with a previously scheduled day off for regular Chase Meidroth.</p><p>"It's really quality at-bats, where he's making good swing decisions, really grinding," Venable said of his newest rookie.</p><p>While Schultz joins a starting rotation that has been surprisingly sturdy, a stagnant Sox offense is desperate for a spark from Antonacci. He joined a team sitting dead last in baseball in batting average (.192), on-base percentage (.281), slugging percentage (.305), hits (107) and runs (54).</p><p>Antonacci’s call-up was hastened by his .313/.500/.479 (15-for-48) start with the Knights, with two doubles, two home runs, seven RBI and five stolen bases.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: 2 teen girls arrested, accused of battering Cook County sheriff's deputies
entries.summary: <p>Two 15-year-old girls were arrested after allegedly battering Cook County sheriff's officers responding to reports of gunfire in Woodlawn Wednesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The sheriff's officers were in the 6400 block of South Evans Avenue at 4:41 p.m. when they saw several people fighting. When they tried to intervene, the two teens allegedly battered the officers, police said. The teens were arrested at the scene.</p><p>One officer was taken to St. Bernard Hospital in good condition, police said.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Nico Hoerner, Matt Shaw dominate as Cubs grab series win over Phillies
entries.summary: <p>PHILADELPHIA —<b> Matt Shaw</b> and <b>Nico Hoerner</b> formed quite the duo in the Cubs' Wednesday’s 11-2 win.</p><p>Shaw would double, and Hoerner drove him in.</p><p>Hoerner's table-setting ways have been pronounced in the last two games of the Phillies series. His eight RBIs over the past two games were the most he’s recorded over a two-game span. The offense is at its best when it strings together hits and has productive at-bats, particularly from the bottom of the order. On all three of Shaw’s doubles, Hoerner drove him in.</p><p>“I thought it was a big night for Matt,” manager Craig Counsell said. “When your No. 9 hitter gets three doubles, that's a good sign.”</p><p>Hoerner was 3-for-5 with a career-high five RBIs. Shaw was 3-for-4 with two RBIs. The ideal version of the Cubs’ lineup involves production from the entire lineup. With first-round picks at six spots, the group has the pedigree and talent to be a problem on a daily basis.</p><p>If the hitters start producing towards their career norms then the offense should be able to carry the bulk of the responsibility while the pitching staff is depleted.</p><p>“We should go out there and expect to have good at-bats,” Shaw said. Things are starting to fall a little bit, so t's awesome to get some momentum and have the boys run.”</p><p><b>Imanaga dealing</b></p><p>As of late, left-hander<b> Shota Imanaga </b>has resembled the pitcher who took MLB by storm in 2024.</p><p>Wednesday’s start got off to an inauspicious start. Imanaga allowed a leadoff homer to Trea Turner, but that was the extent of the damage he allowed Wednesday. Imanaga regrouped and mowed through the Phillies’ lineup. He allowed one run on three hits with one walk and 11 strikeouts. His four-seamer sat at 92 mph.</p><p>“We talk so much about velocity in general,” Hoerner said, “I think it is different with him throwing 93 instead of 90. Every bit of life on that four-seamer he has is a huge deal.”</p><p>Imanaga is pitching with the confidence he seemingly lost toward the end of last season. His 26 whiffs were tied for the most in one outing by a Cubs pitcher in the pitch-tracking era — <b>Yu Darvish</b> also recorded 26 against the White Sox in 2020.</p><p><b>Injury report</b></p><p>The Cubs’ injury report seemingly grows longer by the day. Cubs manager <b>Craig Counsell </b>announced that right-hander <b>Porter Hodge</b> would miss the rest of the season after having UCL reconstruction surgery.</p><p>• Opening Day starter <b>Matthew Boyd</b> is headed to Ohio and will pitch on Thursday for Triple-A Iowa. That puts him on schedule to return to the Cubs around next Wednesday to finish a seven-game homestand against the Phillies.</p><p>• Left-hander <b>Jordan Wicks</b> (left elbow inflammation) is scheduled to pitch Saturday for Triple-A Iowa. He’s been out since spring training.</p><p>• Right-hander<b> Hunter Harvey </b>(right triceps inflammation)<b> </b>is likely going to take longer than the 15 days on the IL. Counsell that Harvey is in strengthening mode.</p><p>• Right-hander <b>Phil Maton</b> (right knee tendinitis) had an optimistic update. Counsell said he’s recovering each day. Phil didn’t stop throwing after he was placed on the 15-day IL, so now it’s a matter of getting the arm back to game action.<br></p>

entries.title: Jed Hoyer to 'come up with real options' for Cubs' injured pitching staff
entries.summary: <p>PHILADELPHIA — Injuries have put <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer on the prowl for starting pitching.</p><p>“You just immediately feel sorry for the player, but then you just process like, ‘Who’s up next?’ ” Hoyer said before the game Wednesday against the Phillies. “You have to move on quick mentally. It sounds cold-hearted, but that’s the nature of the job. The games go on, you have to find replacements.”</p><p>Cubs manager Craig Counsell announced that right-handed reliever Porter Hodge suffered a setback recovering from a flexor strain and will miss the rest of the season after undergoing surgery on his ulnar collateral ligament. He began the season on the 15-day injured list and was seen as a player who could help the team.</p><p>Hodge, whom the Cubs thought could rebound from a rough 2025 season (6.27 ERA), now joins promising right-hander Cade Horton as pitchers lost for the season. Hoyer said that Hodge felt some discomfort early in spring training.</p><p>With relievers Ethan Roberts (middle finger laceration), Hunter Harvey (right triceps) and Phil Maton (knee) all sidelined, the Cubs’ bullpen has become increasingly unbalanced with an unusually large number of left-handers. Given the sheer number of injuries, it’s fair to wonder if the Cubs are assessing their own pitching processes.</p><p>“You have to take a look because you wouldn’t be doing your job if you didn’t,” Hoyer said. “A lot of guys go down these days. Guys throw so unbelievably hard, but we’ll do a deep dive and see if there’s a commonality to the injuries.”</p><p>Entering Wednesday, Cubs relievers had the 15th-best ERA in baseball (4.04). Left-hander Riley Martin has helped the Cubs survive this stretch (4„ scoreless innings).</p><p>Hoyer said that the club is looking at the injuries as an opportunity for others to emerge. Hodge wasn’t on the Cubs’ radar early in the 2024 season, but he received a chance to show how he could deliver in the majors and ran with it (1.88 ERA).</p><p>“There’s opportunities being created for guys,” Counsell said. “Through this process, we’re going to find some guys that are going to help us this year, and so that’s how you’ve got to look at it. That’s a great thing. That’s a positive out of all this.”</p><p>The offense’s improvement also should help the pitching staff. The way hitters were aggressive and opportunistic in Tuesday’s 10-4 win over the Phillies is how many envisioned the offense before the season. Right-hander Colin Rea, who pitched six innings and allowed three runs, said the offensive production made it easier for him to pitch.</p> <p>“Somehow, our run-scoring numbers aren’t that bad,” Hoyer said. “But I think [when] we look up and down the lineup, you have so many guys that are so far below career norms, especially in [slugging] — I look at it as a real opportunity. I’m almost excited about it because we’re 17 games in [and] only a couple guys are sort of above their projections.”</p><p>As the offense finds its footing, Hoyer has to survey the market for capable replacements.</p><p>“The schedule’s not gonna stop,” Hoyer said. “We gotta find ways to come up with new guys and come up with real options. Hopefully, some of those guys can step up.”</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Blackhawks owner Danny Wirtz announces contract extension for GM Kyle Davidson
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" >Blackhawks</a> owner Danny Wirtz announced a multi-year contract extension Wednesday for general manager Kyle Davidson, who's wrapping up his fourth season in the position.</p><p>GM contracts are generally extended consistently until they're fired — it's rare to see one leave an NHL team simply because his contract expired — but it's still notable.</p><p>Wirtz also gave Davidson a firm and extensive vote of confidence on the Chicago Sports Network pregame show.</p><p>"Kyle has done everything we've expected of him," Wirtz said. "When he got the job, his first task was to rebuild our prospect pool. ... He very systematically, very confidently built that to where I believe, right now, we have the best prospect pool in the NHL. Many of those prospects are now actually NHL players, contributing and highly impactful on our team."</p><p>"But at the same time, we didn't hire Kyle to be the prospect GM. He's building a championship-caliber team. It goes to the point we've extended Kyle's contract. We are committing to Kyle to continue the plan he's put in place. We feel confident in that. We believe has the right insight, right team around him and the belief he can continue to build a championship team."</p><p>In a news conference later, Wirtz mentioned the Hawks being more competitive on the ice this season, improving their point total despite losing a plethora of close games, as a sign of improvement.</p><p>Of course, that competitiveness hasn't held true over the past month, during which time the roster has most closely resembled the long-term roster. But Wirtz said he wasn't alarmed by that.</p><p>"[It's] probably a reminder and a recognition of just how hard this league is, especially for players going from leagues where they play considerably less games, less travel," he said.</p><p>"I don’t think that, in any way, shakes my confidence for the team that’s being built... I expect them to continue to grow next season."</p><p>He conceded he would be disappointed next season if the Hawks "stayed flat to this year" and finished in the league's bottom-five again.</p><p>And he clarified Davidson has a green light to make significant trades this summer if the opportunity arises: "There’s nothing holding Kyle back, that’s for sure. It’s not coming from me."</p><p>But he continues to focus most of his attention well into the future.</p><p>"These players, in their own development, have to take another step," Wirtz said. "Even Connor [Bedard] needs to take another step, and he will. He’s that competitive. </p><p>"The collective improvement each of those players makes translates into team competitiveness and ultimately wins. That’s what we’re going for. Our intention is to be competing for and winning Stanley Cups, but we can’t race to that conclusion until we do all those right things."</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module entries.title: 2 teens shot, 1 fatally, at Woodlawn bus stop
entries.summary: <p>Two teens were shot, one fatally, at a bus stop in Woodlawn Wednesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The teens, a boy and girl, both 16, were at a bus stop in the 6300 block of South Stony Island Avenue at 3:23 p.m. when a person approached and opened fire, police said. The boy was hit multiple times and taken to University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition; he later died.</p><p>The girl was shot in her left leg and also taken to University of Chicago Medical Center in fair condition, police said. No one is in custody.</p><p></p><p>Chicago Police Supt. Larry Snelling addressed recent incidents of violence involving young people during a hearing on the federal consent decree Tuesday.</p><p>“We have young kids who are now taking to the streets, not only in Chicago but across the country ... and they’re engaging in activity that has led to violence,” Snelling said.</p><p>Snelling said the police department had seen "more CPS students shot and killed this year than we have in the past 10 years, possibly." According to Chicago Police Department homicide data, 2026 is on track to see the third consecutive year in which youth homicides have fallen by mid-April with 13.</p><p>The city saw 13 youth homicides by this point in the year in 2019 and 2020, though that number nearly doubled in 2023, reaching 24. The tally for the same time period dropped in 2024 and has continued to decline since. Annually, youth homicides have also been declining for several years.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2021/12/20/22836535/cps-trauma-public-schools-student-murders-killed-pandemic-lavizzo-simeon-crown" >Murders of students amid the pandemic strain schools’ ability to cope, heal</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/01/01/chicago-crime-murder-homicide-shooting-president-trump-mayor-johnson" >Chicago records fewest annual killings since 1965</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: Blackhawks end season with feel-good comeback win over Sharks
entries.summary: <p>The first two periods of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' season finale Wednesday mirrored their last few weeks: Sloppy, slow and worrying.</p><p>Then a lucky goal off Sam Rinzel's stick late in the second period shifted momentum, and it seemed the Hawks suddenly discovered an extra reserve energy tank, racing away for a 5-2 win over the Sharks.</p><p>They dominated the third period, getting two beautiful goals from Louis Crevier, two assists from Connor Bedard (both saucy backhand passes) and a redemption goal by Ryan Greene, who had missed an empty net earlier.</p><p>"We wanted to finish on a good note, even though the last couple weeks have been hard," Crevier said. "It doesn't erase what happened, but we showed some character in the third."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Bedard sets up Crevier for the game-tying goal 😮‍💨 <a href="https://t.co/qgpUIGRr6H">pic.twitter.com/qgpUIGRr6H</a></p>— Blackhawks on CHSN (@CHSN_Blackhawks) <a href="https://twitter.com/CHSN_Blackhawks/status/2044606274117988549?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 16, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Wednesday's result marked the first time the Sharks, demoralized after getting eliminated from playoff contention Monday, lost in regulation after leading at the second intermission all season. </p><p>It also marked just the Hawks' fourth win in their last 18 home games. They finished the season 29-39-14, earning 72 points — up from 61 last season.</p><p>"We were never checked out or anything like that," Bedard said. "We were trying every game. That’s something we want people to know. Obviously [it] didn’t go our way, but there wasn’t a day where we weren’t trying to do everything we can to put out our best effort.</p><p>"Coming into this last game, we really wanted to...show our fans just how much pride we have in playing in the NHL but also playing in Chicago. I’m happy we were able to do that and have a win to end the year."</p><p>Crevier delivered a heroic performance, not only with the two goals but also two crucial blocks on a third-period penalty kill, as he bounced back from what he called one of his worst performances of the season <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/13/blackhawks-sabres-effort-levels-crash-frank-nazar-ryan-greene" target="_blank" >Monday</a> against the Sabres.</p><p>His evolution from seventh defenseman into top-four regular was one of the more satisfying under-the-radar trends of this Hawks season. As coach Jeff Blashill put it, "Mental toughness is a huge part of individual success."</p>

entries.title: After another season of strong Blackhawks attendance, it's time to start rewarding fans with more wins
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>’ business department entered this season confident that attendance would be strong, and it was proved correct.</p><p>The Hawks averaged 18,949 fans per game, which ranked fifth in the NHL — behind only the Canadiens, Panthers, Lightning and Red Wings — despite the team finishing 31st in the standings.</p><p>After trending below last season’s average of 18,585 (Winter Classic excluded) for the first month, they ended up easily topping it. </p><p>That’s because since Nov. 23 — the start of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2025/12/01/blackhawks-attendance-ticket-sales-united-center-nhl-sharks-wild" target="_blank" >Thanksgiving week</a> — they averaged 19,440 fans per game, dipping below 18,000 only four times. The United Center was full on a remarkably consistent basis.</p><p>This sets a new high-water mark for the Hawks in the five seasons with full capacity since the pandemic, which ended their 535-game sellout streak. Their 18 sellouts this season mark another post-pandemic high.</p><p>"It has been a few years of not making the playoffs...[but] our fans are still behind us for all 41 home games, and that’s pretty special," Connor Bedard said Wednesday. "You see some teams go through similar things, and they don’t have many people in the crowd. We’re extremely lucky."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2d0000" It’s amazing. I coached in a great sports city — Detroit is a great sports city — [but] this is unbelievable. I can’t wait to win with this group here because it’s such a great fan base.”</p><p>So did Hawks rookie Anton Frondell during his home debut March 31 — after playing his first four NHL games on the road.</p><p>“On the road trip, when we played in Madison Square Garden and different arenas, I thought, ‘Oh, [wow], this is pretty good,’” Frondell said that night. “But they said, ‘Wait until you get back home.’ I know what they mean by that now. It’s a pretty good crowd here.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Jeff Blashill: "I thought our fans were awesome. It was a fun atmosphere to be a part of. Given where we’re at and it’s Game 82, it just speaks so much of our fan base." <a href="https://t.co/G49ZpkauBp">https://t.co/G49ZpkauBp</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://twitter.com/BenPopeCST/status/2044628923191857658?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 16, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The business department was confident in the Hawks’ attendance because of a major draw beyond the on-ice product: centennial season celebrations.</p><p>Not only did more than 20,300 fans attend each of the four special nights, but there was a spillover effect on the season as a whole.</p><p>Advertisements for the centennial were ubiquitous around the city, from bus stops to billboards to O’Hare airport gates. Most people influenced by those ads bought tickets for whatever game best fit their schedule, regardless of its specific programming.</p><p>There also was excitement surrounding the new black alternate sweaters (those six games averaged 19,869 fans) and a nationwide surge in hockey interest after the Winter Olympics. A lot worked in the Hawks’ favor this season.</p><p>Those same advantages won’t exist next season. The Connor Bedard novelty factor has worn off, too. More than at any other point since the pandemic, the Hawks will be dependent on their on-ice product convincing fans to come.</p><p>Yes, they have worked hard to reach a younger generation and broader demographics of fans during the rebuild, which theoretically has expanded the pool of people exposed to hockey and interested in buying tickets.</p><p>Approximately 40% of ticket-holders this season were new fans, and the membership renewal rate for next season currently sits at 95%, according to the Hawks.</p><p>But it’s about time the Hawks start teaching those new fans about the satisfaction of winning — and start rewarding their longtime fans’ support.</p><p>The lack of noise during lineup introductions this season, even from full houses, revealed how little emotional connection fans have with Hawks players. And too often, those full houses went home disappointed by those players’ performance.</p><p>The responsibility to change that partly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/12/blackhawks-vision-next-season-summer-improvement-connor-bedard-ryan-donato" target="_blank" >falls on the players</a>. It falls more heavily on newly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/15/blackhawks-kyle-davidson-contract-extension-danny-wirtz" target="_blank" >extended</a> general manager Kyle Davidson, who might not have many opportunities to bolster the roster from outside this summer but needs to be aggressive whenever they arise.</p><p>His success or failure likely will be seen more vividly in the Hawks’ attendance — and ticket revenue — next season.</p>

entries.title: Man fatally shot, another wounded during brawl in Chatham apartment
entries.summary: <p>Three guns were found inside an apartment late Wednesday where one man man was fatally shot and another was wounded during an argument in Chatham.</p><p>Around 10:40 p.m., several men were inside an apartment in the 7900 block of South Saint Lawrence Avenue when an argument became physical, Chicago police said. </p><p>During the fight, someone fired shots and struck two men before fleeing, officials said. </p><p>A 30-year-old man was shot multiple times in the leg and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he died, police said. A second man, 31, was shot in the neck and was taken to the same hospital in good condition. </p><p>Three handguns were recovered at the scene, authorities said. </p><p>Area 2 detectives were investigating. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: State police fatally shoot armed suspect during domestic incident in Woodlawn
entries.summary: <p>Illinois state police fatally shot an armed suspect during a domestic incident Wednesday night in Woodlawn on the South Side. </p><p>State troopers responded to the 6500 block of South Champlain Avenue around 10:50 p.m. for a domestic battery and encountered the armed suspect where "a struggle ensued in which shots were fired and the suspect was struck by gunfire," state police said. </p><p>The suspect was taken to an area hospital where they were pronounced dead, officials said. </p><p>A gun was recovered from the scene. </p><p>The ISP Division of Internal Investigation Special Agents are investigating the shooting. </p><p>No officers were injured. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Dear Abby: Sister claims late mother changed her estate plan in secret
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My mother passed away recently. She suffered from dementia and was a cancer survivor, but she lived well into her 80s. It was difficult for me to witness her mental decline when I spoke to her on the phone or visited her occasionally in the nursing home. She lived near my sister, so my sister had a much closer relationship with her than I did.</p><p>Mom met with my sister and me several years ago to discuss her estate planning. Both of us were included as beneficiaries, as well as Mom's second husband. My sister has just informed me that, three years ago, Mom replaced the existing living trust with a new one making her the sole beneficiary. She smugly claimed that she was always there for Mother and that I was an absentee child.</p><p>I was stunned to learn this while still recovering from the loss of my mother. I contacted a trust attorney, who told me I could contest the new trust on the grounds that Mother had dementia when it was prepared and that my sister may have coerced her to make her the sole beneficiary.</p><p>If I pursue a lawsuit, it will undoubtedly drive a wedge between my family and my sister's family. On the other hand, doing nothing does not seem fair to my family. Please let me know what you think I should do. — <i>SON IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR SON:</b> I cannot decide this for you. What I "think" is that you should discuss this with your spouse (if you haven't already), decide how much you need the money you were originally promised and proceed from there. Regardless of what you do, your relationship with your sister will never be the same because of this.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'd like to offer some advice to shy people like me. I didn't have a girlfriend until I was 30, although I had my share of female friends. (I met a couple of women in online chat communities.) I tried a bowling league in my 20s, but the bowlers were three times my age. Then I met someone online who introduced me to country music and country dancing.</p><p>Dancing wasn't just a fun activity, but I made a lot of friends, dated a couple of women and met my life's match. We have been married for 17 years now. If you don't know the dances, there are beginners' nights where you can learn. As a guy, I always had a numbers advantage because many women want partners to dance with. My advice would be to try it with no expectations. Abby, I hope this helps someone. — <i>STILL DANCIN' IN PENNSYLVANIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR STILL DANCIN':</b> So do I because your message resonates with me. Years ago, I had a wonderful personal assistant, Olivia. She was born and raised in the great state of Texas and had a love of all things western. Looking to get into the dating scene, one weekend Olivia went solo to a square dance, and that's where she met an "angel" who volunteered to dance with unescorted ladies. Long story short, they were married two months later. I was her matron of honor.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>Good advice for everyone — teens to seniors — is in "The Anger in All of Us and How to Deal With It." To order, send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Anger Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Federal Media Matters probe is an attack on free speech
entries.summary: <p>In November 2023, about a year after Elon Musk took over Twitter, Media Matters for America made a splash with a <a class="Link" href="https://www.mediamatters.org/twitter/musk-endorses-antisemitic-conspiracy-theory-x-has-been-placing-ads-apple-bravo-ibm-oracle" target="_blank" >report</a> claiming that the platform, by then rebranded as X, was "placing ads for Apple, Bravo, IBM, Oracle, and Xfinity next to pro-Nazi content." Musk responded by <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/legal/x-corp-file-lawsuit-against-media-watchdog-others-musk-2023-11-18/" target="_blank" >threatening</a> a "thermonuclear lawsuit" against Media Matters, while Stephen Miller, now a White House deputy chief of staff, <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/StephenM/status/1726281362108538955" target="_blank" >suggested</a> that "conservative state attorneys general" should investigate the organization for "fraud."</p><p>Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey took Miller's advice, launching investigations that were ultimately <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.263967/gov.uscourts.dcd.263967.37.0.pdf" target="_blank" >blocked</a> by federal courts on <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.263967/gov.uscourts.dcd.263967.71.0_1.pdf" target="_blank" >First Amendment grounds</a>. But after those threats fizzled out, the Federal Trade Commission began <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/06/12/the-ftc-risks-chilling-speech-with-its-advertising-boycott-investigation/" target="_blank" >its own probe</a> of Media Matters — a <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cadc.42318/gov.uscourts.cadc.42318.2160563.0.pdf" target="_blank" >blatant assault</a> on freedom of speech at the center of a <a class="Link" href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/71146258/media-matters-for-america-v-ftc/" target="_blank" >case</a> that a federal appeals court <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B3c-nLLFBoI" target="_blank" >heard</a> on Monday.</p><p>To recognize the <a class="Link" href="https://www.cato.org/sites/cato.org/files/2026-02/Media%20Matters%20for%20America%20v%20FTC.pdf" target="_blank" >danger</a> posed by the FTC's investigation of Media Matters, you do not have to like the left-leaning group or accept its critique of X. Whatever the merits of the organization's advocacy, it is indisputably protected by the First Amendment.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-800000" name="module-800000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson nevertheless seems to view speech that discourages businesses from placing ads on certain platforms as evidence of a crime. Ferguson signaled that attitude even before President Donald Trump picked him to run the FTC in December 2024.</p><p>When Marc Andreessen — like Musk, a major Trump donor — <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/pmarca/status/1855024291571790186" target="_blank" >complained</a> about "the orchestrated advertiser boycott against X" that November, Ferguson, then a member of the FTC's Republican minority, <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/AFergusonFTC/status/1855065186899742796" target="_blank" >agreed</a> that "concerted refusal to deal can violate the antitrust laws." </p><p>Touting his qualifications for the job that Trump later gave him, Ferguson<a class="Link" href="https://perma.cc/A56K-Q4YM" target="_blank" > bragged</a> about his "track record" of "standing up" to "the radical left" and promised to "investigate and prosecute collusion" on "advertiser boycotts."</p><p>As FTC chairman, Ferguson brought in several vociferous critics of Media Matters as senior staff members. And in May 2025, four months after Ferguson took office, Media Matters received a sweeping civil investigative demand from the FTC, which sought a long list of internal documents, including financial records and sensitive journalistic material.</p><p>The FTC, which has no authority to regulate nonprofit organizations such as Media Matters, initially did not explain the justification for those highly invasive and burdensome demands. But after Media Matters challenged the civil investigative demand in federal court, the commission said it was investigating "potentially unlawful advertiser boycotts."</p><p>It was not clear why the FTC thought Media Matters had any records relevant to that inquiry. And last August, U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.281859/gov.uscourts.dcd.281859.34.0_1.pdf" target="_blank" >concluded</a> that the commission's putative motive, like the rationales for the Texas and Missouri probes, looked like a cover for unconstitutional retaliation against Media Matters.</p><p>Sooknanan issued a preliminary injunction against the FTC's investigation, saying "Media Matters is likely to show that retaliatory animus was the but-for cause of the FTC's CID (civil investigative demand)." Although the FTC is now <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cadc.42318/gov.uscourts.cadc.42318.01208810356.0.pdf" target="_blank" >asking</a> the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to overturn that injunction, its arguments reinforce the impression that the commission targeted Media Matters because of the views it had expressed.</p><p>"Even publicly available information makes clear why Media Matters might receive a CID in an investigation into advertiser boycotts," the FTC's lawyers <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cadc.42318/gov.uscourts.cadc.42318.01208770012.1.pdf" target="_blank" >say</a>. "For example, Media Matters' website calls for an advertiser boycott even today. Moreover, Congressional testimony has suggested that Media Matters participates in deplatforming and demonetization campaigns."</p><p>That supposed evidence "confirms that the FTC is simply targeting Media Matters for speech," the organization <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cadc.42318/gov.uscourts.cadc.42318.01208822502.0.pdf" target="_blank" >argues</a>. According to the <a class="Link" href="https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep458/usrep458886/usrep458886.pdf" target="_blank" >Supreme Court</a>, it notes, "the First Amendment protects the right to engage in politically motivated boycotts as a means of encouraging social change."</p><p>Media Matters says the FTC's investigation has hurt the organization financially by scaring away donors and deterred it from pursuing journalistic projects that might irk Ferguson or his allies. The chilling impact of Ferguson's vendetta belies his perverse <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/AFergusonFTC/status/1855065186899742796" target="_blank" >claim</a> that he is protecting "Americans' freedom of speech."</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ae0000" name="module-ae0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Chicago shines with short movies about disabilities, finding community at annual Latino Film Fest
entries.summary: <p>Area creatives are leaning into local storytelling through short documentaries and stories that celebrate differences and community in the 42nd annual Chicago Latino Film Festival.</p><p>This year’s film festival, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/04/12/chicago-latino-film-festival-movies-what-to-see" >kicking off Thursday,</a> features four locally produced films, including a short from the nonprofit youth media company Free Spirit Media, as well as a film that resulted from a collaboration between Deep Focus Entertainment and Mass Epiphany Studios. </p><p>In total, the festival spotlights 51 feature films and 31 short films from Latin America, the Caribbean, Europe and the United States. All screenings, including the opening and closing night features, are held in Lake View at the Landmark’s Century Centre Cinema, 2828 N. href="https://latidofilms.com/films/deaf/" target="_blank" ><u>“Sorda”</u></a> on April 17 at 7:45 p.m. and April 26 at 3:15 p.m.</p><p>Abel Berumen’s life changed when he woke up blind as a result of a rare genetic condition called pseudoxanthoma elasticum. Essentially, the transmission between his eyes and brain is being interrupted by the disease.</p><p>Years after losing his vision, Berumen met DePaul University professor <a class="Link" href="https://www.bzahm.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Brian Zahm</u></a> in an experimental filmmaking class and learned about his blindness and incredible photography career.</p><p>Zahm asked if he could gain access to Berumen’s archives to make a documentary about his life, and the 20-minute short “Abel” was born. Berumen was in his mid-50s when he got up in the middle of the night to use the bathroom and, suddenly, he couldn’t see anymore. “Everything was darker than dark,” he said.</p><p>For decades, Berumen worked as a commercial fashion photographer. He’d traveled to New York City and Miami for dozens of photoshoots and even opened a small studio in the Flat Iron building in Wicker Park for his personal work.</p><p>But being blind meant he couldn’t work anymore, and friends and colleagues began disappearing one by one. Berumen felt angry and alone, except for the one bright spot in his life: his partner of more than 30 years, Gia.</p><p>He’s since been able to see and experience life in new ways.“Life doesn't stop, actor Benjamin Delgado, who was five at the time of filming, as her son. The short film is a collaboration between local companies Deep Focus Entertainment and Mass Epiphany Studios.</p><p>The film is a 17-minute short inspired by the real story of director Erick Juarez’s 7th birthday. That year, Juarez’s mother decided that she’d no longer be baking cakes for her children’s parties. She (and everyone around her) got tired of burnt or undercooked cakes, so the logical solution was to buy one.</p><p>The short film, set in Pilsen, follows Rosy and Alex throughout the city as they head to a fancy bakery to get the last-minute dessert in an effort to make young Alex’s birthday the best one yet.</p><p>They end up at the real-life Bittersweet Pastry Shop & Cafe on West Belmont Avenue, where “Chicago Fire” actor Joe Minoso plays the part of the head baker.</p><p>He makes an exception for the mother-son duo on Alex’s special day, even though things don’t exactly unfold to plan.</p><p>“It is the story of me and my mom and how our community came together that day,” Juarez said. He said he hopes the short film reminds viewers of the importance of “kindness that we have for each other.”</p><p>“We know it, we just need a little bit of a reminder. We just need to see it,” Juarez said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-960000" April 23 at 5:30 p.m. and April 24 at 5:15 p.m.</p><p>Filmmaker Ashley Ephraim partnered with Tamika Lycheé Morales, founder of the Autism Hero Project, to tell a story that began developing over a decade ago.</p><p>When Morales’ son was diagnosed with autism in 2015, she blamed herself and “went through all the stages of grief.” There was also a sense of shame attached to the diagnosis. “I didn't tell those who were closest to me,” she said.</p><p>But after some time, Morales began to see her son’s diagnosis as a positive and wanted to help create an accepting, inclusive world for her son.</p><p>She founded the Autism Hero Project, which has since provided medical grants, competency training for first-responders and legislative advocacy. The organization hired Ephraim to work as a video editor for the Autism Hero Project’s annual galas.</p><p>Eventually, Emphraim’s film company BrightCap Entertainment helped make “Created with Purpose.”</p><p>The 20-minute documentary focuses on local autistic individuals and how their families, neighbors and law enforcement can help create a more equitable world for those on the spectrum.</p><p>“We wanted to redefine how people see autism without erasing the reality of it,” Morales said. “Because the truth is, autism is not just one experience. p.m.</p><p>Leiana Carrasco-Ramos wrote and starred in “Lluvia,” another locally produced film making its world premiere at this year’s film festival.</p><p>The 11-minute short tells the story of Lluvia, a young Latina woman working in corporate America. After getting passed up for a promotion, feelings of past trauma and prejudice begin bubbling up to the surface.</p><p>Carrasco-Ramos drew on real-life experiences with racism and fatphobia for “Lluvia,” adding that she wrote the script years ago during a “really angry time in my life.” “I felt really hopeless and trapped,” she said. “I feel like it's a big metaphor for letting out that aggression and that anger.”</p><p>The bloody thriller comes from Free Spirit Media, a West Side arts and media nonprofit for youth ages 11 to 25. Director Nathan Suggs and Carrasco-Ramos met through the writers’ cohort and agreed to work together on the film.</p><p>Ultimately, the film’s goal is to respond to workplace discrimination and silencing that young Black and brown women face daily, Carrasco-Ramos said.</p><p>“For the girls that are too afraid to get angry, who are too afraid to speak up, don't be,” she said, “because your voice matters.”</p>

entries.title: Alexa Rice enters the beauty biz, on her own terms
entries.summary: <p>On a recent Thursday morning, Alexa Rice paces inside a West Side photography studio, adjusting accessories and stepping in and out of frame as models hit their marks for the camera. In jeans, zebra print booties, and a vermilion t-shirt, Rice holds an easy and convivial command of the room.</p><p>“Oh, I love your tattoos,” says Rice, eyeing one makeup artist’s arm. “Oh! Yours too,” she adds, spotting the videographer’s designs. “I feel left out. The way my mother would never talk to me again if I got a tattoo.”</p><p>All around the aspiring beauty mogul, the Humboldt Park space has been transformed into a canopy of greenery, the setting for a marketing shoot launching the 37-year-old’s new Beech Beauty brand. When it’s time for Rice to take center stage, she quickly locks in. Rice is good in front of the camera, too.</p><p>Nearby, her mother, Linda Johnson Rice, in an elegant navy set and notably tattoo-free, soaks in the scene. “There’s something about this room,” she says. “I can feel it. It’s like Alexa’s grandmother is here with her, smiling ear to ear.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a History Museum, ICHi-040405; Stephen Deutch, photographer</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In a culture obsessed with beauty, Rice’s grandmother was a defining force in Black cosmetics and fashion. Eunice Johnson created the Ebony Fashion Fair, and Rice’s grandfather, John H. Johnson founded Johnson Publishing Company and became one of America’s first Black self-made millionaires. Rice was raised inside one of the most influential Black business dynasties in American history, and in a family that helped establish Chicago as a center of Black economic and cultural life.</p><p>At its peak, the Johnson empire included “Ebony” and “Jet”<i> </i>magazines,<i> </i>which together counted millions of readers; Eunice’s traveling runway show, Ebony Fashion Fair, that brought couture to Black America; and her cosmetics line of the same name.</p><p>Fashion Fair was one of the first luxury beauty brands created specifically for Black women in an industry that had largely overlooked them. But as fate would have it, Rice wouldn't inherit the brand, which at its 1980s peak was carried in more than 1,500 department stores nationwide.</p><p>That reality now leaves her trying to build something of her own, in a market that has shifted dramatically. Starting Beech Beauty, says Rice, is a way to "feel closer to my family, and my grandmother specifically. And it's a way to continue our legacy."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ee0000" name="image-ee0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/937d7eb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/450x253+0+39/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb0%2F4a%2Fc2457fc147b69efff2c34dd162a7%2Fimg-1658.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c66e660/2147483647/strip/true/crop/450x253+0+39/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb0%2F4a%2Fc2457fc147b69efff2c34dd162a7%2Fimg-1658.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5f5bf26/2147483647/strip/true/crop/450x253+0+39/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb0%2F4a%2Fc2457fc147b69efff2c34dd162a7%2Fimg-1658.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Alexa Rice (center) with grandparents Eunice Johnson and John H. Johnson. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Alexa Rice</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>A front row seat to an empire </b></h3><p>As a kid, Rice — who radiates warmth and is quick to laugh, often at herself — didn’t fully register the scope of her family’s clout and impact. When asked about her grandparents, she starts small: her grandfather dropping to one knee so she could run into his arms (“I was a large child,” she laughs); her grandmother’s reading and spelling drills (“She was big on education,” she says); evenings spent watching “Murder, She Wrote” from the couch.</p><p>But Rice’s world was undeniably rarified, too. She remembers visiting the White House in 1996 when President Bill Clinton awarded her grandfather the Presidential Medal of Freedom. She had a precocious understanding of Valentino designs, and recalls wearing coveted Chanel flats to class at the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools. There were framed letters from the Kennedys and her mother’s annual Christmas party with a guest list that included criminal defense attorney Johnnie Cochran, all star athlete Bo Jackson, and future president and first lady Barack and Michelle Obama. Rice’s parents separated when she was young. Her father, André Rice, is the founder and president of a fund-of-funds private equity firm.</p><p>At one such party, when Rice was 11, she discovered she was allergic to cashews. Groggy from a heavy dose of Benadryl, Rice woke up to a familiar face.</p><p>“I said, who the hell is that?” laughs Rice. It was Michael Jordan, in 1999, at the peak of his powers, checking in on her. “He was around all the time.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-320000" name="image-320000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/feb0b27/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2077x1166+0+119/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2Fb4%2Fc4925a4845229a618c8858b5bde1%2Fphoto-alexa-and-papa-oct-90-mar-28-2025-19-59-p1.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c0cb6d7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2077x1166+0+119/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2Fb4%2Fc4925a4845229a618c8858b5bde1%2Fphoto-alexa-and-papa-oct-90-mar-28-2025-19-59-p1.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/85e731a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2077x1166+0+119/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2Fb4%2Fc4925a4845229a618c8858b5bde1%2Fphoto-alexa-and-papa-oct-90-mar-28-2025-19-59-p1.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Alexa Rice and grandfather John H. Johnson, who founded Johnson Publishing Company and became one of America’s first Black self-made millionaires.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Alexa Rice</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Rice also witnessed the empire unravel at close range. In the early aughts, Linda Johnson Rice, who took over as CEO at Johnson Publishing in 2002, faced a fast-changing publishing industry. Print advertising declined, subscriptions dwindled, and the company struggled to adapt to the digital era. In 2010, Linda sold the company’s Michigan Avenue offices, one of the first major downtown buildings designed and owned by Black Americans, and once a visible marker of her family’s success. In 2016, Clear View Ventures, a Black-owned private equity firm, bought both “Ebony” and “Jet.”</p><p>In 2019, Johnson Publishing filed for bankruptcy. The remaining assets, including an archive of more than four million photographs, were put up for sale through a court-supervised liquidation. The entire episode “was a very, very difficult and painful decision,” says Linda. “Really gut-wrenching, personally and professionally.”</p><p>One loss, however, was particularly crushing for both Linda and Alexa.</p><p>Fashion Fair, Eunice Johnson’s pioneering makeup line, had been more than a business; it was a living extension of Alexa’s grandmother. In November 2019, as part of the bankruptcy proceedings, the brand sold at auction for $1.85 million to an investor group led by former Johnson Publishing executive and close family friend, Desiree Rogers, along with Cheryl Mayberry McKissack, another Johnson Publishing alum.</p><p>Alexa says she and her mother believed there had been an understanding with Rogers that neither would bid on Fashion Fair during the bankruptcy proceedings. The pair were shocked to learn that Rogers was part of the group that ultimately acquired the company.</p><p>Linda prefers not to dwell on the episode. “That’s done for me,” she says. “People are gonna do what they’re gonna do, and there are things you can’t control. I cannot let that drag me down.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d80000" name="image-d80000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0d7311f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1989x1116+0+942/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2F92%2Fceb860d1450e9badfd85e5e16a2a%2Fap921101096.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/029c7bc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1989x1116+0+942/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2F92%2Fceb860d1450e9badfd85e5e16a2a%2Fap921101096.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b8a36f0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1989x1116+0+942/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2F92%2Fceb860d1450e9badfd85e5e16a2a%2Fap921101096.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="John H. Johnson poses with daughter Linda Johnson Rice at the Johnson Publishing Co. headquarters in Nov. 1992.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>AP Photo/Mark Elias</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Alexa, however, is more emotionally forthright. “It was the biggest devastation and betrayal I have felt,” she says. “I could not believe it. I was heartbroken.”</p><p>At the time, Alexa was a graduate student at Harvard Divinity School — for a while, she considered joining the ministry — and found herself sitting with that grief. “Divinity School is not a bad place to receive devastating news,” she reflects. “If you’re going to crash out, I recommend being with people who are training to be priests, pastors, and rabbis.”</p><p>Asked for her characterization of events, Desiree Rogers, now CEO of both Fashion Fair and Black Opal Beauty, another cosmetics brand for women of color, responded in an email: “JPC no longer owned the company when we bid [on] it. We were surprised and delighted that our bid was selected and that it would remain in the hands of African Americans.”</p><p>Looking back, Alexa says the experience clarified something for her: she and her mother may have lost Fashion Fair, but no one could take away the years Alexa spent at Eunice’s side, or what her grandmother taught her about color, skin, and a deep, enduring love of beauty.</p><p>“You can own the business,” says Alexa, “but you can’t own my grandmother.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-130000" name="module-130000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><b>Johnson Publishing Company: a brief timeline</b></h3><br><b>1942</b> — John H. Johnson founded Johnson Publishing in Chicago with a $500 loan and launched “Negro Digest.”<br><br><b>1945</b> — “Ebony” debuted; at its peak, the magazine reached millions of readers, becoming a central chronicle of Black life.<br><br><b>1951</b> — “Jet” launched. The weekly digest became known for its coverage of the Civil Rights movement, including the publication of Emmett Till’s open-casket photos.<br><br><b>1958</b> — Eunice Johnson launched the Ebony Fashion Fair, which raised more than $55 million for Black organizations over five decades.<br><br><b>1971</b> — The company opened its custom-designed headquarters on South Michigan Avenue, one of the few downtown buildings owned by a Black company at the time.<br><br><b>1973</b> — Fashion Fair Cosmetics was introduced, one of the first major beauty lines for women of color; at its height, the brand was sold in 1,500 department stores across the United States.<br><br><b>2002</b> — Linda Johnson Rice took over as chief executive of Johnson Publishing.<br><br><b>2010</b> — Johnson Rice sold the Michigan Avenue headquarters, marking the end of an era for the company.<br><br><b>2016</b> — “Ebony” and “Jet” sold in 2016 to a private equity firm as debt mounted.<br><br><b>2019</b> — Johnson Publishing filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy, listing millions in liabilities and including as assets its archive of more than 4 million photographs.<br><br><b>2022</b> — A consortium of foundations commit $30 million to digitize the photography archive and make it publicly available through National Museum of African American History and Culture and the Getty Research Institute.<br><br><b>2026</b> — Alexa Rice lays groundwork for her new brand, Beech Beauty, writing a new chapter in her family story.</div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Look good while doing good </b></h3><p>Enter: Beech Beauty.</p><p>The idea first came to Rice in her final year at Harvard, where she had been studying how disparities in green space shape city life. Rice wanted to find a way to connect those issues with the lessons she had absorbed from her family. So, as her final thesis project, Rice proposed a beauty brand that would donate a portion of sales to planting trees in underserved communities.</p><p>“My mom always says, why not look good while doing good?” Rice reflects.</p><p>The project was also inspired by Eunice, who raised over $55 million for Black organizations through Ebony Fashion Fair.</p><p>In 2023, Rice decided to give Beech a real shot. She chose to start small, with her own money, and from an office in her Gold Coast apartment. (Rice declined to say how much she has invested, but calls the amount “significant.”) Later this year, she will debut a line of lip glosses in seven shades, each named for a flower, along with a sweatshirt, both sold direct-to-consumer through the Beech <a class="Link" href="https://www.beechbeauty.com/" target="_blank" ><u>website.</u></a> And true to the original project, a portion of sales will go toward combatting environmental inequity.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink"
