And it’s a way to continue our legacy.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Alexa Johnson Rice</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Alexa is not interested in just being an heiress,” says visual artist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/art/2025/09/19/theaster-gates-art-smart-museum-university-of-chicago-unto-thee-rebuild" target="_blank" ><u>Theaster Gates,</u></a> a close family friend and steward of the Johnson Publishing library, which is housed at his Stony Island Arts Bank on the South Side. “She is thinking about ways she can have a significant life and make a significant impact in the world. It’s a beautiful thing when a person finds the balance between recognizing the history they come from and not being burdened by it.”</p><p>Building the brand has been a process of trial and error. “I have done everything myself. I’ve gotten comfortable sending cold emails and making cold calls,” says Rice. “The worst that happens is they either don’t reply or they say no — I’ll live.”</p><p>Rice's first move was buying what she calls an “obscene” number of lip glosses, and testing how they wore over time. When Rice figured out what she liked — moisturizing with good color payoff — she found a California manufacturer and started working on her own formula. Rice was especially careful about how colors read on Black and brown skin. “A vibrant purple is going to show up so differently on me than it will on someone who looks like Lupita Nyong’o,” says Rice. “I wanted the shade range to take into account as many skin tones as possible.”</p><p>It took multiple iterations, she says, to create a product that felt inclusive, playful and bold. “This whole clean girl aesthetic, it’s just not for me,” says Rice, laughing at the current fad of dewy, fresh-faced minimalism. “I don’t know her. I wish her luck. She’s in my prayers, but that’s just not who I am.”</p><p>The result is a saturated lip gloss with a nourishing, emollient base that feels high-end, packaged with a ’70s-meets-millennial flair.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b50000" name="image-b50000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3df5f1d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd6%2Fd1%2Fbae4997743ad9f1255129d672863%2Falexajohnsonrice-2604050012.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5f5bc9a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd6%2Fd1%2Fbae4997743ad9f1255129d672863%2Falexajohnsonrice-2604050012.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b65886a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd6%2Fd1%2Fbae4997743ad9f1255129d672863%2Falexajohnsonrice-2604050012.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Alexa Rice, founder of Beech Beauty, granddaughter of John H. Johnson and Eunice Johnson poses for a portrait in the Johnson Publishing Company library and archive at the Stony Island Arts Bank in Chicago, Illinois on March 12, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b65886a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd6%2Fd1%2Fbae4997743ad9f1255129d672863%2Falexajohnsonrice-2604050012.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2b95703/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd6%2Fd1%2Fbae4997743ad9f1255129d672863%2Falexajohnsonrice-2604050012.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b65886a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd6%2Fd1%2Fbae4997743ad9f1255129d672863%2Falexajohnsonrice-2604050012.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“I take the privilege, the uniqueness, and all the lessons of my upbringing in this family with me,” Rice said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Connecting the past with a bright new future</b></h3><p>Rice jumps into the beauty market at a moment when a spin through Sephora or Ulta feels like a red carpet award show. And while the market is huge — projected to surpass $700 billion globally this year — it is also crowded with everyone from conglomerates to celebrities like Hailey Bieber and Selena Gomez.</p><p>And it’s hard for Black founders to break through. According to Crunchbase, a database that tracks venture capital activity, less than 1% percent of all venture funding went to startups with a Black founder in 2024. The brief surge of support for Black-owned businesses post-George Floyd’s 2020 murder has largely receded.</p><p>None of this deters Rice because, she asserts, “if I’m not going to bet on myself, who will?”</p><p>Part of launching Beech Beauty, says Rice, has been launching herself. Over the past few years, the affable, droll founder has built a sizable following on social media, posting videos that toggle between stories about her grandparents, makeup tutorials, research on urban infrastructure, and lessons she’s learned while building a brand.</p><p>In one video, Rice lines her lips while detailing a new city ordinance aimed at addressing environmental racism. In another, she models Bob Mackie designs from her grandmother’s closet as she narrates the history of Ebony Fashion Fair. (Her impression of Wendy Williams as an owl is also a delight.)</p><p>Across her platforms, Rice’s aim is clear: connect her family’s past to a new chapter that is wholly her own.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-620000" name="html-embed-module-620000"></a><blockquote class="tiktok-embed" cite="https://www.tiktok.com/@alexachristinarice/video/7275830860039851306" data-video-id="7275830860039851306" style="max-width: 605px;min-width: 325px;" > <section> <a target="_blank" title="@alexachristinarice" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@alexachristinarice?refer=embed">@alexachristinarice</a> Replying to @james Redlining is just one branch on the massive redwood tree that is environmental racism, but i hope this helps. I will definitely be revisiting this topic in the future becasue there’s a lot to say. Follow for more urban environment content! <a title="urbanforestry" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/urbanforestry?refer=embed">#urbanforestry</a> <a title="urbanforest" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/urbanforest?refer=embed">#urbanforest</a> <a title="environmentaljustice" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/environmentaljustice?refer=embed">#environmentaljustice</a> <a title="environmentalracism" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/environmentalracism?refer=embed">#environmentalracism</a> <a title="redlining" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/redlining?refer=embed">#redlining</a> <a title="treeequity" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/treeequity?refer=embed">#treeequity</a> <a title="forestry" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/forestry?refer=embed">#forestry</a> <a title="urbanplanning" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/urbanplanning?refer=embed">#urbanplanning</a> <a title="arborist" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/arborist?refer=embed">#arborist</a> <a title="arboristsoftiktok" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/arboristsoftiktok?refer=embed">#arboristsoftiktok</a> <a target="_blank" title="♬ original sound - Alexa Rice | Beech Beauty💄🌳" href="https://www.tiktok.com/music/original-sound-7275830918559583018?refer=embed">♬ original sound - Alexa Rice | Beech Beauty💄🌳</a> </section> </blockquote> <script async src="https://www.tiktok.com/embed.js"></script> </div> </div><p>From her apartment, set against a backdrop of taxidermy tiger skin (one of many expressions of her family’s shared fondness for animal print), Rice has begun planning Beech’s rollout for later this year. She will soon head to Los Angeles with her mother, who is developing several film and television projects based on the Johnson story.</p><p>A few years ago, Rice briefly considered moving to Los Angeles and building her business from there. The plan didn’t stick. “Chicago is where my family is, and it’s where I want to be,” she says. “My grandparents built their business here, so why can’t I?”</p><p>Any new endeavor, especially from a family like the Johnsons, will inevitably come with scrutiny. “There will be comparisons, there always are,” says Linda Johnson Rice. “But you don’t know if something can be a home run until you get up at bat. Alexa comes from a family that swings.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f10000" name="image-f10000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e4c9094/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F63%2F0c%2F32056bc14b6c8720c08a64a83803%2Fobamacenter-111625-007.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4ddbd00/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F63%2F0c%2F32056bc14b6c8720c08a64a83803%2Fobamacenter-111625-007.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eab62e4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F63%2F0c%2F32056bc14b6c8720c08a64a83803%2Fobamacenter-111625-007.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The Obama Presidential Center is under construction in the historic Jackson Park neighborhood on the South Side, Wednesday, Nov. 5, 2025. The centerpiece is the museum building, clad in light-colored, New Hampshire granite." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eab62e4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F63%2F0c%2F32056bc14b6c8720c08a64a83803%2Fobamacenter-111625-007.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2223382/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F63%2F0c%2F32056bc14b6c8720c08a64a83803%2Fobamacenter-111625-007.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eab62e4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F63%2F0c%2F32056bc14b6c8720c08a64a83803%2Fobamacenter-111625-007.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Theaster Gates’s forthcoming installation, a large-scale collage of Johnson Publishing images celebrating Black womanhood, will soon be on view at the Obama Presidential Center. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Both Rice’s Beech Beauty and her mother’s new projects arrive at the same time as Theaster Gates’s<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/art/2026/03/19/obama-presidential-center-contemporary-art-collection-barack-michelle-virginia-shore" target="_blank" ><u> forthcoming installation</u></a> at the Obama Presidential Center, a large-scale collage of Johnson Publishing images celebrating Black womanhood. In addition, a consortium of foundations has committed $30 million to digitize the enormous “Ebony” and “Jet”<i> </i>photography archive and make it publicly available through National Museum of African American History and Culture and the Getty Research Institute.</p><p>The timing feels almost serendipitous, with the resurgence happening seven years after the bankruptcy filing. After all, the Johnson Publishing case was only finalized earlier this year.</p><p>As the only Johnson grandchild, that history can, at times, weigh heavily. But Rice doesn’t frame it that way. “I don’t take the weight,” she says. “I take the privilege, the uniqueness, and all the lessons of my upbringing in this family with me.” And that, adds Rice, no one can buy.</p>

entries.title: Record Store Day returns to Chicago this weekend with live bands, exclusive pressings and $1 deals
entries.summary: <p>Record Store Day is an annual tradition that, while celebrated around the country, gets special treatment in Chicago. This Saturday, expect more than three dozen shops in the area to fete the day with live events and fresh pressings, including a 20th-anniversary release from a-Ha and famed private recordings of John Coltrane’s band by musician Frank Tiberi in the ‘60s.</p><p>Chicago’s independent record stores know how to celebrate, often drawing lines around the block — some even starting Friday night. Here are 10 you may want to check out this weekend.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.beverlyrecords.com/home.htm" target="_blank" ><u>Beverly Records</u></a></h3><p><b>Hours:</b> 8 a.m. - 6 p.m.<br><b>Address: </b>11612 Western Ave.</p><p>With its 60th birthday next year, Beverly Records is an institution. Every Record Store Day the store opens its doors two hours earlier than usual; this year's special programming includes a visit from the cast of The Goodman Theatre’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/04/08/review-ma-raineys-black-bottom-goodman-theatre" target="_blank" ><u>“Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom.”</u></a> The performers will kick off the day with a ceremonial needle drop of <a class="Link" href="https://recordstoreday.com/SpecialRelease/20160" target="_blank" ><u>a collection of Rainey’s blues hits</u></a> (among the exclusive titles on sale for Record Store Day) and a raffle of tickets for the show. Customers can also get White Castle sliders and 20% off used vinyl.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.bridgeportrecords.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Bridgeport Records</u></a></h3><p><b>Hours:</b> 10 a.m. - 10 p.m.<br><b>Address: </b>3251 S. Halsted St.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DW1tLCpERCA/" target="_blank" ><u>Enjoy live DJ sets</u></a> and check out a pop-up from Illinois-based Prairie Cannabis.</p><div entries.title: Cash-strapped DePaul closes the curtain on Downtown's historic Reskin Theatre
entries.summary: <p>For nearly 120 years, the Merle Reskin Theatre has hosted everything from "Pygmalion" and "Life With Father" to "Mirror of Most Value: A Ms. Marvel Play," which opens mid-May for a two-week run.</p><p>What's playing after May? Darkness. And not the 2021 Andre Wright play with the same name, either.</p><p>DePaul University is closing the Reskin at the end of next month.</p><p>The university says it's the result of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/10/17/fewer-international-students-are-studying-at-some-illinois-universities" target="_blank" >budget crisis</a> that has been aggravated by the Trump administration's immigration policies that has reduced the amount of tuition-paying international students attending the school.</p><p>Also part of DePaul's budget troubles: The decision in February to close the respected <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/03/02/depaul-university-art-museum-closure-fullerton-lincoln-park-students-faculty-letter" target="_blank" >DePaul Art Museum</a> at 935 W. Fullerton Ave.</p><p>"The university is working to determine the future use of the Merle Reskin Theatre," a DePaul spokesperson said in a statement.</p><p>But until that use is found, it's lights out for the Reskin, 60 E. Balbo Drive. The decision places in limbo a landmarked 1,400-seat Beaux Art playhouse designed by Benjamin H. Marshall, one of Chicago's preeminent architects.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" of the Reskin's mothballing. "I would pray and hope that some [theater] company would come along and claim it. But given the financial environment in general, I fear that it will be sitting there for a long time. It seems like it's really up for grabs for its future."</p><h3>Reskin ‘a wonderful asset’</h3><p>Built in 1910 as the Blackstone Theatre, the venue sits in the western shadow of the 21-story Blackstone Hotel, which was also designed by Marshall and completed in 1910.</p><p>Marshall and his firm Marshall & Fox designed scores of notable buildings around town, including the South Shore Cultural Center, 7059 S. South Shore Drive, and the Drake Hotel, 140 E. Walton St.</p><p>For much of the 20th century, Marshall's ornate Blackstone theater — with its columned entrances and mansard roof — and his elegant Second Empire-styled Blackstone Hotel were a swank brother-and-sister act that drew the best plays, conventions and events.</p><p>Legendary actors including John and Ethel Barrymore, Spencer Tracy and Helen Hayes performed at the Blackstone during the good years.</p><p>The venue closed in the mid-1980s and was bought by DePaul for its theater school.</p><p>A $2 million donation from businessman Harold Reskin and wife, Merle, who had been an actress, singer and dancer, helped refurbish what would open in 1992 as the Merle Reskin Theatre.</p><p>Merle Reskin died in 2023. Harold Reskin passed away in 1996.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-780000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Architectural details enliven the facade of the Merle Reskin Theatre.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The theater's French-inspired auditorium remained intact, although it has faded somewhat in recent decades. The Reskin is home to DePaul Theatre School's Chicago Playworks for Families and Young Audiences.</p><p>DePaul said the Chicago Playworks series will continue this fall at the Theatre School building in Lincoln Park.</p><p>"That DePaul, which is really such a great school and it's got a great theater department, will be bereft of this wonderful asset," Lepauw said of the Reskin, "l think it's just so sad."</p><h3>What’s next?</h3><p>Whatever the Reskin's fate, it won't be demolition. The theater is listed as a contributing structure in the landmark-protected 12-block long Historic Michigan Boulevard District.</p><p>For DePaul, money is tight. But tight is relative: The university managed to come up with enough scratch to start construction this year on a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/11/20/plan-commission-approves-depaul-practice-facility-morgan-park-commons" >$42 million</a> basketball and athletics center on its Lincoln Park campus.</p><p>It should be equally diligent in finding the funds to preserve, restore and reuse the Reskin. The city shouldn't lose a live entertainment venue anywhere, particularly Downtown.</p><p>And Chicago certainly doesn't need a dark, unused building glowering over Balbo Drive.</p><p>But suppose DePaul finds it no longer wants the Reskin. Then finding a new owner who can restore the theater and put it in league with Downtown's Chicago, Nederlander and Cadillac Palace theaters becomes paramount.</p><p>Rich Gamble, interim CEO of the Chicago Loop Alliance, said his group has been talking to DePaul about the Reskin. The university is a member of the downtown organization.</p><p>"I'm not in a position to explicitly state the nature of those conversations," Gamble said. "We're a supporter, an advocate and a promoter of what we would like to see happen, which is a vibrant district."</p>

entries.title: Chicago’s school board election is coming. Here’s what to know and what’s at stake.
entries.summary: <p>Soon, voters will elect all 21 members of the Chicago School Board for the first time.</p><p>It’s a significant shift for the governing body, which was under mayoral control for decades. The city <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2024/06/04/what-you-need-to-know-about-chicagos-elected-school-board" target="_blank" ><u>held its first-ever school board elections</u></a> in 2024, but that year only 10 seats were up for grabs. The rest, including the board president, were appointed by Mayor Brandon Johnson.</p><p>The change marks the culmination of years of work by advocates who pushed for an elected board, arguing that it would inject democracy and community voice into the board’s decision-making. Though there are concerns that <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/02/19/big-money-expected-to-flow-in-novembers-historic-chicago-school-board-race" target="_blank" ><u>big money expected to flow</u></a> in this year’s races will undermine that.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatLeft><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-dd0000" name="module-dd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><hr><h3>Tell us your questions for Chicago’s school board candidates!</h3><br>Whether you’re a Chicago Public Schools parent or a Chicago taxpayer, the future of our city’s school system affects you.<br><br>That’s why WBEZ, the Chicago Sun-Times and Chalkbeat Chicago want to know what issues matter the most to you — and what questions you have for school board candidates. Your responses will shape our community-driven elected school board voter guide, to be released this fall.<br><br><a class="Link" href="https://airtable.com/appu9nu8BNBrotoOR/pagRg1TV9UI2TfPGd/form" target="_blank" ><u>Take the survey here.</u></a><br><br><a class="Link" href="https://airtable.com/appu9nu8BNBrotoOR/pag9iBoUzH3Dpvjlw/form" target="_blank" ><u>También está disponible en español aquí.</u></a><br><hr></div> </div><p>There’s also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/12/08/few-residents-know-chicago-will-have-a-fully-elected-school-board-poll-finds" target="_blank" ><u>gaps in voter awareness to overcome</u></a>. Two out of three Chicago residents didn’t know the board would become fully elected, according to a poll by the nonprofit Kids First Chicago. And many voters don’t know exactly what the school board does.</p><p>Here’s what you need to know about the board’s responsibilities and what to expect in the elections later this year.</p><h3>What does the school board do?</h3><p>The board has several responsibilities, including opening and closing schools, hiring and evaluating the CPS CEO, approving the budget, the school calendar and vendor contracts and deciding which school buildings get upgrades.</p><p>They meet at least twice a month at their headquarters in the Loop and can expect to spend potentially more than 30 hours a month on their duties, according to the board website. But members aren’t paid to serve on the board. Some have raised concerns that lack of compensation discourages parents from low-income households from representing their communities.</p><p>The board also sets academic goals and priorities for the school year. That means members spend time attending community events, hosting office hours and visiting schools to get a sense of what their constituents want.</p><h3>How will the election work?</h3><p>For the upcoming election on Nov. 3, the city has been divided into 20 subdistricts. Residents will vote for one candidate to represent the area where they live. (<a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/about/chicago-board-of-education/member-map/" target="_blank" ><u>You can look up your school board subdistrict here</u></a>.) But everyone will be able to vote for the school board president, which is a citywide seat.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/sites/cps-policy-rules/bylaws/chapter-1/1-3/" target="_blank" ><u>The terms of the newly elected members</u></a> aren’t all the same because of the board’s transition from being partially elected to fully elected.</p><p>Candidates who win races for seats currently held by appointed members will serve two-year terms. Those who win seats currently held by elected members will serve four-year terms. The board president will serve for four years.</p><p>From there on, elections will be held every two years so only half the seats are up for election at a time.</p><h3>When will I know who’s running for the school board?</h3><p>The window for interested candidates to get their names on the ballot is open. Each elected board member must live within the subdistrict they represent. Board member candidates need 500 to 1,500 valid signatures to enter the race. Those running for school board president have to submit at least 2,500.</p><p>Interested candidates began collecting signatures on Feb. 24. They have to submit their paperwork by May 26, at which point voters will know who the candidates are, though <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/chicago-school-board/2024/07/02/more-than-half-of-chicago-school-board-candidates-face-ballot-challenges" target="_blank" ><u>some will likely face ballot challenges</u></a>.</p><p>The list of candidates will be finalized by Aug. 27, when the county clerk must certify the election ballot.</p><h3>Will campaign contributions be important in this election?</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/02/19/big-money-expected-to-flow-in-novembers-historic-chicago-school-board-race" target="_blank" ><u>Many expect spending</u></a> in this year’s school board elections to exceed what was spent on the first-ever school board race in 2024. That came out to $13 million, <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2025/01/27/ctu-incs-spent-millions-on-school-board-races/" target="_blank" ><u>according to a Chalkbeat Chicago analysis</u></a>.</p><p>But with twice as many district seats at stake this year, plus a citywide campaign for board president, many more dollars may pour in.</p><p>Labor-backed and pro-charter school factions are expected to play a role like they did in the 2024 elections. The business community, which has come out strongly against Mayor Brandon Johnson and his allies on the school board, could also factor in.</p>

entries.title: Car insurance premium inequities are driven by age, credit and ZIP code, study finds
entries.summary: <p>It's well known that auto insurance companies charge more to people who have caused crashes or have had a DUI.</p><p>But the companies also charge more to customers over other factors they have less control over: age, credit and their ZIP code.</p><p>Those factors play a large role in customers' premiums and disproportionately affect older adults, low-income and working families, according to a new study commissioned by the Illinois secretary of state's office.</p><p>The study, released Thursday, found:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-afe8fb62-38df-11f1-bbb7-7d41cfb5a997"><li>Drivers with poor credit can pay more than 2.7 times higher premiums than someone with excellent credit.</li><li>Older adults can face substantially higher rates despite a safe driving record. Drivers ages 80 to 84 pay up to 72% more for bodily injury coverage than drivers in their mid‑50s.</li><li>Drivers in certain ZIP codes can pay more than 2.5 times higher rates than those in other parts of the state, even when all other factors are the same.</li></ul><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dd/09/a0718bd8456e99c06d22959e5d82/orcaa-auto-insurance-rates-study.pdf" target="_blank" >study</a>, conducted by New York-based auditing company O'Neil Risk Consulting & Algorithmic Auditing, backs up Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias' push for a bill that he says would rein in car insurance costs that are unfairly discriminatory.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus/FullText?GAID=18&DocNum=1486&DocTypeID=SB&LegId=160057&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >bill</a>, which passed the state House in March and is awaiting a Senate vote, would require the Illinois Department of Insurance to review auto and home insurance rate hikes over 10% and order refunds for customers it determines were overcharged. The state could contest proposed hikes if they are "excessive, inadequate, or unfairly discriminatory."</p><p>Every other state in the nation has similar laws to review rate hikes except for Illinois and Wyoming, according to Giannoulias' office.</p><p>"This study puts hard data behind what Illinois drivers have been experiencing for years — pricing practices that can penalize people for factors beyond their control," Giannoulias said in a statement.</p><p>A series of recent insurance rate hikes has spurred the debate over insurance premiums. Gov. JB Pritzker sparred earlier this year with Bloomington-based State Farm in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2026/01/23/pritzker-pushes-back-at-state-farm-in-escalating-fight-for-tighter-insurance-regulations" target="_blank" >calling for tighter regulations</a> after homeowner insurance premiums rose an average of 27% last summer.</p><p>Car insurance premiums in Illinois rose 18% in 2024, according to Giannoulias.</p><p>But car insurance companies argue that the bill would destabilize the state's insurance market and actually result in higher premiums. After the bill passed the state House in March, a coalition of insurance companies issued a statement saying it represented the "most sweeping and harmful insurance regulatory overhauls in state history."</p><p>The insurance companies noted that the bill ignores that auto insurance rates in Illinois are 18% below the national average. Rates are also declining in Illinois due to fewer crashes and claims, contrary to rising rates nationally, according to the companies.</p><p>"I think [the insurance companies] are scaremongering," said Abe Scarr, director of the consumer advocate group Illinois PIRG. His group wants to outlaw the use of race and credit, among other factors, in setting insurance premiums. </p><p>The House-approved bill does not do that, he said. At most, the state could use the "unfairly discriminatory" language to reject rate hikes that rely on factors like credit ratings, Scarr said. But it's not clear if that will happen.</p><p>"I haven't seen this used in other states for this purpose, so we'll see how that's used here," Scarr said.</p><p>It's unclear when the bill could receive a Senate vote in Springfield.</p><p>Giannoulias' study focused on how “multiplicative factors” in premium rate-setting result in pricing disparities.</p><p>For instance, someone living in the 60426 ZIP code that covers south suburban Harvey would pay a bodily injury premium more than 2½ times higher than someone living in the downstate ZIP code 62379 in Warsaw, all other factors being the same.</p><p>When considering age, the study found that a base rate bodily injury premium of $100 would jump up to $118 for a 70-year-old and up to $172 for an 80-year-old.</p><p>Giannoulias' study also includes nearly 2,000 responses from residents. He's been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/07/29/secretary-state-alexi-giannoulias-aarp-car-insurance-price-discrimination" target="_blank" >collecting community feedback</a> over the last year through his office's “Driving Change” campaign.</p><p>Among those giving feedback was Algia W., an older adult from Oak Lawn. She said her family's premiums have gone up yearly despite them never filing a claim. Her insurance company told her that was due to the rising number of claims in her area.</p><p>"We are close to retiring soon, and there is no way we could afford this coverage on a fixed income!" she said. "Why are WE paying higher premiums because of where we live?"</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/5/17/18623979/car-insurance-roulette-higher-price-factors-illinois" target="_blank" >2019 Sun-Times investigation</a> found that being a woman, living on the “wrong” side of two adjacent ZIP codes, renting rather than owning your home, or working in an unskilled job could result in a higher price quote for car insurance.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/10/18/nonstandard-car-insurance-consumer-complaints-american-alliance-first-chicago-insurance-united-equitable-american-heartland" >Illinois’ most complained-about car insurance companies and how consumers can protect themselves</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

A new virtual reality experience lets Chicagoans to strap on a headset and explore a digital recreation of that fateful voyage. Sun-Times reporter Stefano Esposito gave it a go. </p><p><b>What it's like</b>: "Titanic: A Voyage Through Time" is an immersive experience that gives you the sensation of being in a three-dimensional world while wearing a virtual reality headset as you traipse through a giant gallery space in Old Town. Guests start out exploring the wreck, and then they're led — by members of the crew — to different parts of the ship, above and below deck, as it makes its way toward disaster.</p><p><b>If you go</b>: You'll find the "Titanic" experience at 108 W. American countries and the U.S. by showcasing international cinema alongside local independent works for two weeks at the Landmark’s Century Centre Cinema in Lake View, starting Thursday and running through April 27.</p><p>After more than 40 years under founder Pepe Vargas’ leadership, the event is the largest and longest-running festival dedicated to showcasing work by Latino filmmakers in the U.S.</p><p>The first-ever feature-length animated movie made entirely in Mexico, "Soy Frankelda," and the opening night feature, "Aún Es De Noche En Caracas" from Venezuela, are two highlights among the 51 feature-length and 31 short films in this year’s festival.</p><p>Several local filmmakers are premiering shorts — written, filmed and produced in the city — at this year’s festival. <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-widjuul-l-tt/" target="_blank" >Learn more about these local titles here</a>.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-widjuul-l-ti/" target="_blank" ><b>FULL FILM FEST PREVIEW HERE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>Yesterday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-widjuul-l-th/" target="_blank" >Should Chicago continue to have delivery robots on the city’s streets?</a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said…</p><p>"I think delivery robots are part of our future. I support them. There have been very few glitches so far, and as far as I know, no one has been injured. The technology will continue to improve. Within a year or two, I doubt anyone will think twice about them." — <i>David Shiner</i></p><p>"Chicago should not have delivery robots. These food delivery jobs are typically the types of jobs that our youth would have as they were finishing high school or during the summer. Additionally, the property damage will only increase, and soon, more people will be injured too." — <i>Dee Crawford</i></p><p>"Delivery robots and autonomous vehicles are just a way for tech companies to drain money out of Chicago and lay off workers. There is no benefit to the local economy." — <i>Mike McMains</i></p><p>"I would take more delivery robots on our sidewalks over the current situation ... our streets are routinely choked with double-parked delivery drivers. A drive along Lincoln Avenue between Webster and Fullerton any evening of the week is chaos!" — <i>Tom Stroud</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia</p><hr><p><i>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you. entries.title: Autoridades en Chicago obtienen la primera declaración de culpabilidad en un caso del Operativo Midway Blitz
entries.summary: <p>Los fiscales federales en Chicago aseguraron su primera declaración de culpabilidad relacionada con el Operativo Midway Blitz el miércoles, aunque no por el cargo de asalto que inicialmente se había presentado contra Anthony González Álvarez.</p><p>En su lugar, se declaró culpable de ocultar información sobre un crimen, admitiendo que reportó falsamente que su Ford F-250 había sido robada al Departamento de Policía de Chicago (CPD) después de chocar contra la parte trasera de un vehículo conducido por agentes de inmigración.</p><p>El cargo, oficialmente conocido como “encubrimiento de un delito grave”, es aparentemente lo suficientemente raro como para haber provocado una discusión en la corte sobre cómo pronunciar "encubrimiento".</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c80000" name="module-c80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Nunca había oído hablar de eso”, les dijo la jueza del distrito LaShonda Hunt a los abogados.</p><p>Se espera que Álvarez, de 27 años, pague $1,362 en restitución, pero evitará la prisión bajo los términos de un acuerdo alcanzado con los fiscales. Sin embargo, Hunt primero debe decidir si acepta o rechaza el acuerdo.</p><p>Ha pospuesto la decisión por ahora y fijó la sentencia para el 22 de julio.</p><p>Álvarez está entre los <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >32 acusados conocidos</a> que enfrentan cargos por crímenes no relacionados con inmigración vinculados al Operativo Midway Blitz, la campaña de deportación que conmocionó el área de Chicago el año pasado. Veinte de los 32 han sido exonerados y otros tres están en camino a que se desestimen sus casos.</p><p>Cuatro de los ocho restantes son miembros del grupo originalmente conocido como los <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/03/13/fiscalia-retira-los-cargos-de-conspiracion-contra-2-manifestantes-de-ice" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six”</a> y enfrentarán juicio el 26 de mayo. Otro hombre, Héctor Gómez, está programado para declararse culpable el 27 de abril tras ser acusado de cargos de armas relacionados con el Operativo Midway Blitz.</p><p>La administración de Trump utilizó afirmaciones de violencia "aterradora" hacia agentes federales para justificar un esfuerzo por desplegar tropas de la Guardia Nacional en Chicago el otoño pasado. Inicialmente fueron bloqueados por la jueza del distrito April Perry y, finalmente, por la Corte Suprema de Estados Unidos.</p><p>A pesar de la declaración de culpabilidad de Álvarez, nadie en Chicago ha sido condenado en una corte federal por un acto de violencia hacia los agentes durante el Operativo Midway Blitz.</p><p>Aún así, Álvarez admitió que a eso de las 10:30 a.m. del 3 de octubre, siguió a un vehículo de la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) en el lado sur de la ciudad. Al girar a la derecha desde la 61th Street hacia Kedzie Avenue, chocó contra el lado trasero del vehículo de los agentes.</p><p>Más tarde ese día, Álvarez le dijo a CPD que su camioneta había sido robada, admitió.</p><p>Álvarez se declaró culpable a pesar de las preguntas planteadas anteriormente sobre el caso por su abogado defensor, Ricardo Meza. El abogado le dijo a Hunt en enero que "la camioneta que supuestamente fue golpeada ha sido reparada".</p><p>"Ni siquiera está en la condición en la que estaba cuando supuestamente fue golpeada por mi cliente, por lo que no podemos inspeccionarla", le dijo Meza a Hunt el 29 de enero. "Pero a pesar de eso, su Señoría, también queremos inspeccionarla porque queremos recuperar lo que se llama el registrador de datos de eventos".</p><p>Meza también dijo que solicitaría las notas de los agentes del Buró Federal de Investigaciones (FBI) porque "hay mucha confusión sobre lo que pasó, cuándo sucedió y cuántas veces fue golpeado un vehículo".</p><p>La asistente del fiscal estadounidense Stephanie Stern le dijo a la jueza que Meza tenía el poder de citar el vehículo él mismo, desde la compañía de alquiler de autos que estaba en posesión del vehículo.</p><p>"Está con Enterprise", dijo durante la audiencia de enero.</p><p>Cuestiones similares surgieron en el caso de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/02/04/marimar-martinez-baleada-por-agentes-de-migracion-se-pronuncia-contra-asesinatos" target="_blank" >Marimar Martínez</a>, la mujer a quien le disparó un agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza el 4 de octubre. Poco después de que la acusaran de chocar contra el vehículo de ese agente, su abogado defensor reveló que el agente había llevado su vehículo a Maine antes de que el abogado pudiera inspeccionarlo. Los cargos en contra de Martínez fueron desestimados en noviembre.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Johnson calls Rahm Emanuel's mayoral record 'disqualifying' for a possible presidential contender
entries.summary: <p>As former Mayor Rahm Emanuel revs up for a 2028 presidential bid, Mayor Brandon Johnson on Thursday described Emanuel’s eight years as mayor as “disqualifying."</p><p>Johnson did not identify Emanuel by name when he talked about the one Democrat in the crowded field of possible presidential contenders whom he would like to, as he put it, “x-out.”</p><p>But there was no doubt about whose potential presidential campaign Johnson was attacking, even before Emanuel has formally announced. </p><p>“I have very deep concerns about the former mayor of the city of Chicago. What he did in Chicago — from school closures to privatization to austere budgets,” Johnson said during his monthly appearance on WBEZ-FM’s “Ask the Mayor” program before a live audience.</p><p>“There was a boy who was murdered by a police officer and it was covered up," Johnson added. "That’s disqualifying for me.” Johnson’s cover-up allegation a was a reference to the 2014 murder of 17-year-old Laquan McDonald by now-convicted former Chicago police officer Jason Van Dyke.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Dashcam video of Van Dyke shooting McDonald sixteen times while the teenager was walking away from the officer with a knife in his hand was withheld by the city until a Circuit Court judge ordered the city to release it fourteen months after the shooting.</p><p>Van Dyke was convicted of second-degree murder and aggravated battery. He was released from Taylorville Correctional Center in central Illinois in February, 2022 after serving less than half of his 81-month sentence.</p><p>In the furor that followed release of the video, Emanuel weathered weeks of protests and unprecedented demands for his resignation before ultimately choosing political retirement over the uphill battle for a third mayoral term. In an attempt to tamp down the controversy, he told the City Council a “code of silence” existed in the Chicago Police Department.</p><p> Johnson’s political broadside came a day after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/04/15/rahm-emanuel-online-betting-prediction-markets-tax-proposal-presidential-bid" >Emanuel appeared</a> at a Wall Street Journal Live event in Washington and floated a 10% federal tax on online sports betting and prediction markets to boost revenue for science and technology. On Thursday, Emanuel refused to respond to Johnson's remarks.</p><p>“I’m not going to engage. Whatever,” Emanuel told the Sun-Times.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-690000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Former Mayor Rahm Emanuel critiqued Democrats and unveiled a plan to tax online sports betting and prediction markets during a Wall Street Journal Live event in Washington on Wednesday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Screenshot</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Former longtime Inspector General Joe Ferguson spent much of his tenure at loggerheads with Emanuel. He reiterated Thursday what he wrote to members of the U.S. Senate’s Foreign Relations Committee who were deciding in 2019 whether or not to confirm Emanuel as U.S. Ambassador to Japan.</p><p>“That is not the fact” that there was a cover-up according to “an evidence-based record that was developed from many forms of inquiry and investigation,” Ferguson said. “And we’re better served not re-litigating controversies of the past..." </p><p>Ferguson said he was not surprised by Johnson’s attack on Emanuel with just a few months to go before Johnson must decide whether or not to seek a second term.</p><p>“In a heightened political environment, we’re always going to hear things like this,” said Ferguson, who now serves as president of the Civic Federation. “The problems of the city are of such magnitude that it’s critically important that all attention be focused on them because we have work to do.”</p><p>A pragmatic centrist who has never backed down from a political fight, Emanuel has long been in the cross-hairs of Johnson and his fellow far-left Democrats.</p><p></p><p>As a paid organizer for the Chicago Teachers Union, Johnson protested Emanuel’s decision to cancel teacher pay raises, triggering the 2012 teachers strike as well as Emanuel’s decision to close 50 schools in one fell swoop.</p><p>Johnson talks often about having “taken an arrest” while protesting Emanuel’s decision to close Dyett High School.</p><p>Last year, Johnson tried to undermine a potential political comeback by Emanuel — accusing the former two-term mayor of having devised and “executed” the anti-Black, neoliberal “playbook” that Johnson says is now being followed by President Donald Trump.</p><p>What rankled Johnson then was watching an interview with Emanuel and being “incredibly bothered by his temerity.”</p><p>At the time, Johnson said there has been a “long, sustained movement” in Chicago to push back against the “neoliberal agenda” that Emanuel championed to “set up austere budgets” targeting African-Americans and the “public accommodations” that support them.</p><p>“The playbook that Donald Trump is running is a playbook that Emanuel executed in this city,” Johnson said then.</p><p>“We didn’t get here because we just happen to have a tyrant in the White House. We got here because someone gave him the script… The shutting of schools. The firing of Black women. Privatizing our public education system is why the system is as jacked up as it is today.”</p><p></p>

entries.title: Hyde Park Academy student was killed in shooting that stemmed from earlier dispute, police say
entries.summary: <p>Sixteen-year-old Eric Billups was fatally shot in an attack that left a Hyde Park Academy High School classmate wounded after the shooter and Billups, who had quarreled earlier, made plans to fight each other after school Wednesday, according to a Chicago police report. </p><p>When school dismissed, Eric and a 16-year-old girl were waiting at a bus stop in the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/15/two-teens-shot-bus-stop-woodlawn-stony-island" target="_blank" > 6300 block of South Stony Island Avenue around 3:25 p.m</a>., police said. </p><p>"The offender confronted the victim at the bus stop, retrieved a handgun from his backpack and opened fire on the victims," according to police reports obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>Eric suffered at least five gunshot wounds to his abdomen, chest and left arm and was unresponsive at the scene. He was rushed to the University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition and pronounced dead at 3:48 p.m., according to the Cook County medical examiner's office.</p><p>Eric's mom was too distraught to speak when reached by a Sun-Times reporter.</p><p>The girl, who was shot once in her calf, was also taken to the University of Chicago, where she was listed in fair condition. </p><p>Witnesses told officers that Eric and the shooter were supposed to fight after school, police reports state. It was unclear what the dispute was about, but the alleged shooter, who had been released from school early, came back still wearing a Hyde Park Academy uniform, according to reports.</p><p>Police found 12 shell casings from a 9 mm gun, two book bags and blood at the scene, the report said.</p><p>The shooting happened two blocks from Hyde Park Academy high school resulting in the school briefly being placed on a soft lockdown, officials said. </p><p>In a letter sent to Hyde Park Academy community members, Principal Rosette Edinburg noted that "some members of our school community were impacted by this incident" and the school was working to offer support services. </p><p>"We will be working with the CPS Crisis Management Unit to provide support to students and staff members. Our own school-based mental health professionals will also be available for students who need ongoing services," the letter states. "We are extremely saddened by this incident and will do everything we can to help our school community heal."</p><p>“All of us at Chicago Public Schools are saddened to learn of the loss of a young person’s life, and we extend our heartfelt condolences to the family, friends, school and community members impacted by this tragedy,” CPS said in a statement. </p><p>Fifth Ward Ald. Desmon Yancy said Thursday morning he was "still processing" the shooting in his ward.</p><p>"It's still difficult to understand how young people are dealing with trauma and grief while still having easy access to handguns," Yancy said. "It's hard for me to think about what goes through the mind of young people where they feel like they have to resolve conflict with violence." </p><p>Yancy noted that it's been a "rough few weeks" for the Hyde Park Academy community. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/girl-15-killed-while-riding-scooter-in-south-shore-hit-and-run" target="_blank" >Violet Harris</a>, a 15-year-old student, was killed after a vehicle crashed into the electric scooter she was riding last month in South Shore and <a class="Link" href="https://abc7chicago.com/post/family-mourning-hyde-park-high-school-student-killed-dolton-hit-run/18828745/" target="_blank" >Lania Smith</a>, 18-year-old senior, was killed in a hit-and-run in Dolton earlier this month. </p><p>"My heart goes out to the community and with community leaders about how we can not only support the students there, but also try to mitigate this violence," Yancy said. </p><p>On Tuesday, Yancy was in attendance at a "parent takeover" after "credible reports" of a teen takeover in Hyde Park from Mayor Brandon Johnson's office.</p><p>"It's better for us to try and find ways to support each other through this moment and at the same time figure out what role you can play in impacting young people so that this violence doesn’t become an option for them," Yancy said. </p><p>Johnson's office didn't comment on the shooting, citing the ongoing investigation. </p><p>No arrests had been made as of Thursday morning. <br></p>

entries.title: Larry Hoover's former Gangster Disciples No. 2 man says he's drowning in debt from court-ordered fine
entries.summary: <p>Gregory Shell was once the right-hand man to Gangster Disciples boss Larry Hoover in a $100 million-a-year drug empire, according to federal authorities.</p><p>Now, he says he’s flat broke. And he's asking a judge to wipe out most of what’s left of his court fine.</p><p>“It’s unfair,” Shell said in an interview. “The interest is more than my original fine, which was $15,000.”</p><p>Shell and Hoover both were sentenced in the 1990s to life in prison for running a drug conspiracy. They were shipped to the nation’s toughest prison, the Colorado “supermax” where the worst of the worst criminals, including former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/07/03/chapo-margarito-flores-pedro-flores-saul-rodriguez-sinaloa-cartel" >Sinaloa cartel</a> boss Joaquín <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/el-chapo" >“El Chapo” </a>Guzmán Loera, are held.</p><p>Last year, they were sprung from the federal prison after winning presidential commutations on their federal convictions. But their legal troubles aren’t over.</p><p>Hoover, 75, is still serving a state life sentence for murder and is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/04/07/gangster-disciples-larry-hoover-gangs-trump-eileen-burke" target="_blank" >asking Gov JB Pritzker for executive clemency</a>. after President Donald Trump commuted his federal sentence.</p><p>Shell, 68, is back at home on the South Side — and back in court, trying to get out of most of the remaining debt from his federal case.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-060000" name="image-060000"></a> <picture 2025 and shaved $10,000 off his $15,000 fine.</p><p>Prosecutors say Shell still owes $1,461 in principal — plus a whopping $20,630 in interest on that — and argue that he shouldn’t be let off the hook.</p><p>Shell might claim to be broke now, but that could change, prosecutors said in a court filing late last month. "Now, the government's insistence on payment of interest that is 20 times what he owes on the original fine is counterproductive and puts a crippling roadblock in Mr. Shell's path to reintegration and entries.title: Trump says Israel and Lebanon have agreed to a 10-day ceasefire
entries.summary: <p>Israel and Lebanon have agreed to a 10-day ceasefire, President Donald Trump announced Thursday, two days after the countries held their first direct diplomatic talks in decades in Washington.</p><p>The truce that Trump said was scheduled to begin at 5 p.m. Eastern follows more than a month of war between Israel and the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in Lebanon.</p><p>Lebanon has insisted on a ceasefire to stop the fighting between Israel and Hezbollah before engaging in more talks, while vowing to commit to disarming the group.</p><p>The president also invited the leaders of Israel and Lebanon to the White House for what he said would be “the first meaningful talks" between the countries since 1983.</p><p>“Both sides want to see PEACE, and I believe that will happen, quickly,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.</p><p>Lebanon and Israel signed an agreement in 1983 saying Lebanon would formally recognize Israel, and Israel would withdraw from Lebanon. The deal fell apart during Lebanon’s civil war and was formally rescinded a year later.</p><p>Trump said the pause in fighting followed “excellent” conversations with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.</p><h3>Pakistan army chief meets with Iranian parliament speaker</h3><p>Meanwhile, Pakistan’s powerful army chief met Thursday with Iran’s parliament speaker as part of international efforts to press for an extension to a ceasefire that has paused <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/iran" target="_blank" >almost seven weeks of war</a> between Israel, the U.S. and the Islamic Republic.</p><p>It was unclear whether the frantic diplomacy could lead to a lasting deal as the two-week ceasefire passes the halfway mark. The Iran war has killed thousands of people and <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/economy-imf-outlook-iran-war-trump-inflation-growth-e3d8a239509abb50757f8c8d42fb32d8" target="_blank" >upended global markets</a> by disrupting the flow of oil.</p><p>Iranian state television did not provide details on the meeting between Pakistani Army <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/pakistan-iran-us-munir-497734c37c4304d3af958a0c63879d3c" target="_blank" >Gen. Asim Munir</a> and Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, who has emerged as his country’s chief negotiator.</p><p>There was no immediate comment from Pakistan, which has <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/pakistan-us-iran-war-emerging-peace-mediator-f4e809dd3f93b3d67b54f9d75d33d55c" target="_blank" >become a key mediator</a> after hosting direct talks between the U.S. and Iran that authorities said helped narrow differences between the sides. Mediators are seeking a new round before the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/iran-us-israel-trump-lebanon-april-7-2026-421ee64fdc9a5c26460df8119c7d1b3f" target="_blank" >ceasefire expires</a> next week.</p><p>The White House said any further talks regarding Iran would likely take place in the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/islamabad" target="_blank" >Pakistani capital of Islamabad</a>, though no decision had been made on whether to resume negotiations. The fragile ceasefire is holding despite a U.S. naval <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/iran-us-israel-trump-lebanon-april-12-2026-a8a0d22918fc3fb30bc3abf1cd5c5a13" target="_blank" >blockade of Iranian ports</a> and Iranian counter-threats to target regional ports across the Red Sea.</p><p>The war has <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/stocks-oil-bonds-iran-war-gasoline-72cc1c65d842ded41d20f3be48a2acd3" target="_blank" >jolted markets and rattled the global economy</a> as shipping has been cut off and airstrikes have pounded <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/iran-iraq-us-israel-trump-march-18-2026-d7ca062ba1bf99d1f8dc00c8073cf10f" target="_blank" >military and civilian infrastructure</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/stock-markets-trump-oil-iran-war-7659569791b1f5e108489360d18e50f1" target="_blank" >Oil prices have fallen</a> amid hopes for an end to fighting, and U.S. stocks on Wednesday <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/stock-markets-trump-oil-iran-war-7659569791b1f5e108489360d18e50f1" target="_blank" >surpassed records</a> set in January.</p><h3>Lebanese president refuses to speak with Israeli PM</h3><p>During the fragile ceasefire with Iran, <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/lebanon-israel-war-hezbollah-negotiations-394f8bdaee36bab82ab3ebc713221302" target="_blank" >fighting has continued in Lebanon</a> between Israel and the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah.</p><p>Trump had announced that the leaders of Israel and Lebanon would speak about halting the fighting. If that were to occur, it would be the first direct conversation between the leaders of the two countries in more than 30 years.</p><p>But at one point Thursday, Aoun refused to speak to Netanyahu, a government official familiar with the developments told The Associated Press.</p><p>The government official, who spoke on condition of anonymity in line with regulations, said the remarks were made during a call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and that Washington “understands Lebanon’s position.”</p><p>Washington has not publicly stated its support of a ceasefire as a precondition, and the Israeli government has framed the talks as peace negotiations with a focus on disarming Hezbollah.</p><p>Israel and Hezbollah exchanged fire across the border, with Hezbollah targeting towns in northern Israel with rockets and drones. Israeli fire against southern Lebanon intensified, especially around the cities of Tyre, Nabatieh and the strategic town of Bint Jbeil near the border with Israel.</p><p>Israel and Lebanon have technically been at war since Israel was established in 1948, and Lebanon remains deeply divided over diplomatic engagement with Israel.</p><p>Israeli troops have pushed deeper into southern Lebanon to create what officials have called a “security zone,” which Netanyahu has said will extend at least 8 to 10 kilometers (5 to 6 miles) into Lebanon.</p><h3>Officials say US and Iran are making progress</h3><p>Even as the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/iran-war-strait-of-hormuz-blockade-trump-bf6a057faebfc11eb0c76510a4fc20b1" target="_blank" >U.S. blockade on Iranian ports</a> and renewed Iranian threats strained the ceasefire, regional officials reported progress, telling AP that the United States and Iran had an “in-principle agreement” to extend it to allow for more diplomacy. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive negotiations.</p><p>But tensions simmered.</p><p>The commander of Iran’s joint military command, Ali Abdollahi, threatened to halt trade in the region if the U.S. does not lift its naval blockade, and a newly appointed military adviser to Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said he does not support extending the ceasefire.</p><h3>Mediators seek compromise on sticking points</h3><p>Mediators are pushing for a compromise on three main sticking points: Iran’s nuclear program, the Strait of Hormuz and compensation for wartime damages, according to a regional official involved in the mediation efforts.</p><p>Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said Iran is open to discussing the type and level of its uranium enrichment, but his country “based on its needs, must be able to continue enrichment,” Iranian state media reported.</p><p>The Pentagon urged Iran to make a deal, with U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth telling reporters at the Pentagon that “ultimately, they need to come to the table.”</p><p>He said the U.S. will ensure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon.</p><p>“We’d prefer to do it the nice way through a deal led by our great vice president and negotiating team. Or we can do it the hard way,” Hegseth said.</p><p>Iran has repeatedly insisted that it does not seek a nuclear weapon and that its nuclear program is for peaceful proposes.</p><p>The fighting has killed at least 3,000 people in Iran, more than 2,100 in Lebanon, 23 in Israel and more than a dozen in Gulf Arab states. Thirteen U.S. service members have also been killed.</p><p>U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Trump administration would ramp up economic pain on Iran with <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-treasury-bessent-iran-sanctions-f45619d7ea3050bd4b1cdd9c3881ca2b" target="_blank" >new economic sanctions</a> on countries doing business with it, calling the move the “financial equivalent” of a bombing campaign.</p><p>Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met with Qatar’s emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, during a visit to Doha, his office said, as part of a regional visit aimed at discussions on the ongoing U.S.-Iran peace process.</p><h3>China calls for Strait of Hormuz to reopen</h3><p>Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said the window of peace was opening during a phone call with his Iranian counterpart, according to a statement from the Chinese Foreign Ministry.</p><p>Wang told Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi that the situation has reached a critical juncture, and said Iran’s sovereignty, security and legitimate rights should be respected, while freedom of navigation and safety through the Strait of Hormuz should be ensured.</p><p>Since the war began, Iran has curtailed maritime traffic through the strait, which a fifth of global oil transited through in peacetime. Tehran’s effective <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/the-worlds-most-important-21-miles-0000019d2fbfd29daffdefffc72e0000" target="_blank" >closure of the strait</a> sent oil prices skyrocketing, raising the cost of fuel, food and other basic goods far beyond the Middle East, and the U.S. has responded with a blockade on Iranian shipping.</p><p>U.S. Central Command said Wednesday that no ships had made it past the blockade since it was imposed two days earlier, while 13 merchant vessels complied with direction from U.S. forces to turn around and reenter Iranian waters.</p>

entries.title: Concejo Municipal elige al concejal Gilbert Villegas como presidente del comité de zonificación
entries.summary: <p>El <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/03/23/city-council-zoning-committee-chair-vacancy-stalemate-brandon-johnson-jack-lavin" target="_blank" >presidente del Comité de Zonificación del Concejo Municipal</a> quedó en un punto muerto que dejó paralizado 85 proyectos de construcción, y terminó el miércoles con la elección del veterano concejal Gilbert Villegas (36º) para ocupar el cargo y del concejal Derrick Curtis (18º) para reemplazar a Villegas como presidente del Comité de Desarrollo Económico.</p><p>La reorganización fue la última derrota política para el alcalde Brandon Johnson a manos de un Concejo fortalecido que rechazó el impuesto a las corporaciones del alcalde durante el debate del presupuesto de la Municipalidad el otoño pasado. Villegas y Curtis formaron parte de la mayoría rebelde del Concejo que aprobó un presupuesto alternativo desafiando al alcalde.</p><p>El Concejo Municipal tomó cartas en el asunto después de que Johnson no pudo obtener un voto mayoritario para sus dos favoritos anteriores para reemplazar al ahora retirado presidente del Comité de Zonificación, Walter Burnett: los concejales Byron Sigcho López (25º) y Daniel La Spata (1º).</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bb0000" name="module-bb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Sin duda es otro ejemplo de cómo el Concejo interviene y, de alguna manera, rescata un tema para llenar un vacío de lo que no está sucediendo en el Quinto Piso [oficina del alcalde] que es consistente con lo que ocurrió con el presupuesto”, dijo el concejal Marty Quinn (13º), uno de los críticos más vocales de Johnson.</p><p>El concejal Brian Hopkins (2º) dijo que el bloque mayoritario no tuvo más remedio que tomar cartas en el asunto para romper un estancamiento que había detenido en gran medida el desarrollo en Chicago.</p><p>“Es el único comité que simplemente debe reunirse o tendrás este enorme atraso de asuntos legislativos importantes que causaría un daño real permitir que queden en el limbo. No podemos permitir que eso suceda”, dijo Hopkins.</p><p>A finales de noviembre, el presidente interino del Comité de Zonificación, Bennett Lawson (44º), le dio a Johnson un <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/11/18/ald-bennett-lawson-acting-zoning-committee-chair-mayor-brandon-johnson-ultimatum" target="_blank" >ultimátum de fin de año:</a> que hiciera su puesto en el comité permanente con control sobre su propio personal o se retiraría de este trabajo que consume tiempo.</p><p>Lawson se mantuvo firme al negarse a celebrar una reunión del Comité de Zonificación en enero, aunque en febrero presidió una reunión que incluía a Foundry Park, una versión reducida del enorme desarrollo de Lincoln Yards en el lado norte.</p><p>Esperaba convencer a sus colegas de que le otorgaran el trabajo permanente cuando el Concejo Municipal se reunió el 18 de febrero, pero el estancamiento continuó mientras algunos miembros del Caucus Negro promovían a Gilbert Villegas (36º) para hacerse cargo del Comité de Zonificación y al concejal David Moore (17º) para reemplazar a Villegas como presidente de Desarrollo Económico.</p><p>El plan de Lawson para nombrar a dos de sus compañeros concejales de primer año como vicepresidentes también aliñó a los concejales veteranos.</p><p>El miércoles, Lawson esperaba intentar de nuevo, usando una maniobra parlamentaria para forzar una votación inmediata sobre la reorganización que estaba estancada desde hacía tiempo. Pero el plan de Lawson se desmoronó durante negociaciones frenéticas destinadas a romper el estancamiento.</p><p>El concejal Bill Conway (34º) presentó la reorganización revisada negociada por la presidenta del Caucus Negro, Stephanie Coleman (16º), que nombró a Villegas como presidente de Zonificación y a Curtis para reemplazar a Villegas.</p><p>Villegas agradeció a sus colegas por la confianza depositada en él y aplaudió a Lawson por mantener la fortaleza en dos ocasiones, una vez después de que el presidente de Zonificación, Carlos Ramírez-Rosa (35º) <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2023/11/6/23949206/concejal-ramirez-rosa-renuncia-tras-confrontacion-crisis-migratoria-venezuela" target="_blank" >fuera forzado a renunciar</a> por acusaciones de maltratar a un colega concejal, y de nuevo después de la <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/07/17/walter-burnett-son-27th-ward-city-council-seat" target="_blank" >jubilación del decano del Concejo Municipal, Walter Burnett.</a></p><p>“Para aquellos de ustedes que no me apoyaron, quiero trabajar con ustedes para averiguar cómo podemos seguir avanzando la ciudad”, dijo Villegas. “Y tienen mi compromiso de que trabajaremos juntos para asegurarnos de que los proyectos en el vecindario de todos se realicen de manera rápida para poder abordar la vivienda asequible, los precios de mercado y todo otro tipo de construcción”.</p><p>Johnson tomó la derrota del miércoles con calma.</p><p>"La ciudad de Chicago está abierta para los negocios. Simplemente no está en venta," dijo Johnson. "Voy a trabajar con cualquiera que esté comprometido a ayudarnos a construir la ciudad más segura y asequible de Estados Unidos, ya seas progresista o te llames de otra forma. No me detengo en esos títulos ideológicos particulares porque he visto a personas que se autoproclaman ser algo y no lo son", aseguró el alcalde.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Sky sign Megan Nestor to training camp contract
entries.summary: <p>The Sky are rounding out their roster for training camp, which begins on April 19.</p><p>They signed Megan Nestor, a 6-4 forward out of North Texas, to a training camp contract.</p><p>In Nestor's final collegiate season, she averaged a double-double with 12.8 points and 14.1 rebounds per game. Before that she played Wayland Baptist (TX) of the NAIA. </p><p>Nestor grew up in Saint Lucia, an island in the Caribbean. </p><p>The Sky now have 17 players on the training camp roster and can bring 18 players to camp. Twelve will make the final roster, with up to two developmental spots also available. Developmental players can play in up to 12 games and will not count against the salary cap. </p><p>Two remaining roster questions are on Ajša Sivka, the Sky's No. 10 pick in the 2025 draft, and Sevgi Uzun, a 28-year old point guard. Sivka, 20, played overseas last season and general manager Jeff Pagliocca said there is still no decision on whether she's joining the team this season. </p><p>The Sky extended Uzun a qualifying offer but no deal has been made. </p>
